strength: It reads cleanly and leads with the right moves. It brings back 'Dad's razor vs mine' with 2 to 3 new cuts, cuts the Starter Kit on its after-RTO number, and narrows Women Body Razor to 25 to 34. The safe and break-even lines are tied to the 72% UTM match, and the budget adds to exactly ₹5,60,000.
mistake: It applies the Meta-versus-Shopify gap as a single blunt line instead of setting real per-ad-set numbers. It also never says what the whole plan should earn, so I can't see the expected rupee outcome of the 14 days.
to10: Add a projected profit for the plan. Add a prepaid or COD-confirmation fix path for the Starter Kit. Explain why retargeting and DPA should take a heavier attribution haircut.

strength: It is rigorous on store-count profit, with a separate attribution haircut for prospecting and for retargeting. It forecasts the plan's outcome and puts most of the reserve behind release rules. It names concrete first moves for day one and adds a geo-holdout test that would show whether retargeting earns anything at all.
mistake: It brings back the creator video but adds only one Rohan ad, with no new cuts of that hook. It labels retargeting 'cut' while only halving it. The brand guard rule drops the skin-colour and body-hair limits. The dates are invented.
to10: Add 2 to 3 new cuts of the 'Dad's razor' hook. Make the call labels match the actions. List the full brand avoid list. Tighten the wording so the team can read it faster.

strength: A tight, Monday-ready plan. The setup list is clean, the budget table adds to $30,000, and every kill and scale rule is in dollars tied to the $38 target. The day-30 scorecard checks new store customers against TikTok's claimed orders, so it tests whether TikTok adds customers rather than taking Meta's credit.
mistake: The hooks rarely use Maria's or Tasha's exact words; most are paraphrases. It also misses that our trend sound may not be cleared for ads.
to10: Write the hooks in the customers' own lines, such as "My feet don't ache by hour ten." Add a geo holdout as a cleaner incrementality check.

strength: The creative table is built straight from Maria's and Tasha's words, and every number has its working shown. It uses three ways to read day 30 plus a geo holdout. It also catches details I'd have missed: the trend sound isn't cleared for ads, existing customers should be excluded, and there's a learning-budget bar for each ad group.
mistake: The day-21 release rule counts TikTok-reported cost as one of its three votes. The "Where it goes" ad runs the donation line as its on-screen line, which edges toward a mission-led ad. The "Worth $15?" ad puts price up front.
to10: Drop platform-reported cost from the release vote. Make sure the donation line only ever closes an ad. Trim the length a little.

strength: It covers all three signals: skip the belt, lift it yourself and the 5 am quiet wheels. The data reads are sharp (women bring 26% of purchases on 18% of spend), and the primary text is short and calm, in our voice.
mistake: It stops short of production. There are no headlines and no scene timings. The test budget of about ₹4,500 per concept is too thin to judge cost per purchase. Concept 5 also states 'Quiet wheels' as brand copy, which is not an approved spec.
to10: Add headlines and second-by-second scene notes. Set a realistic test budget. Keep 'quiet' and 'light' inside buyer quotes. Put the women's concept first in the pick, since that is where the efficiency is.

strength: It is close to brief-ready for production. It has a recommendation up front and a summary table. Each concept has scene timings, safe zones and headlines with character counts. The claim rules are strict ('quiet' only as a buyer's line), and the per-audience test budget is sensible at about ₹63,000. It also leads the pick with the cheapest audience.
mistake: Some primary text runs long and repeats the spec list, so it reads less like our short-line, grade-7 voice. Concept 7's live scale reading is a risk if the number does not show about 2.6 kg. Calling weekend couples 'unaware' is questionable.
to10: Cut the primary text to three or four short lines. Add a second awareness-level variant for the women's concept. Make sure the scale shot shows the approved weight.

strength: Clean, on-voice scripts with one script built around the 3 pm soda moment. Openings follow my cost-per-purchase data, and it has lines that sound like us, such as "Still fizzy. Still sweet. Still my treat."
mistake: Price, our top objection, is handled only in Script 2. Disclosure sits in the shared rules rather than in each creator brief.
to10: Answer "$3 a can" in every script or explain why not, put the disclosure steps inside each creator brief, and add a budget to the test plan with cut-off rules tied to my numbers.

strength: It is built to run. Price is answered in every script ("12 afternoons for me"), disclosure is both on screen and spoken, and it covers delivery specs, usage rights and timelines. The test plan uses my real spend numbers: $72k total, $800 per ad, and cut-offs at the 19% and $32 marks.
mistake: The spoken disclosure lines ("Olipop paid me for this one") feel clunky and break the playful voice. It also runs close to or over the word limit. The rights terms and the new, untested opener style are presented without being flagged as assumptions.
to10: Let creators disclose in their own natural words, tighten it to fit under 1,300 words, flag the rights and fee terms as assumptions, and make the hook lines a bit more playful.

strength: It reads the data correctly: it brings the paused front-of-pack winner back in new words and puts taste and price in the first four ads. Character counts are shown and accurate.
mistake: Range is thin. Two primary texts are front-of-pack, and taste and texture are near-duplicates. Ad C spends a launch slot on a second transparency variant. Priya's samosa line and the 4 pm hook are mostly unused.
to10: Replace one transparency text with a true 4 pm or samosa angle in Priya's words. Add some wit to the headlines. Give a concrete budget and a decision rule for each cell.

strength: Six genuinely different angles written in Aditya's and Priya's own words, with witty lines like "Your 4 pm, minus the samosa" and "Fair. Here's your ₹90". It adds a launch plan with a control cell, budget maths, kill rules and a fatigue trigger that I could run tomorrow.
mistake: Ad C quotes the price objection in the ad itself. That is risky, though it is flagged as the bold bet. The front-of-pack text P1 carries no number. The ₹6,000 a day budget is an assumption.
to10: Add a number to P1. Offer a safer backup line for the price ad. Confirm that legal allows review quotes in ads.

strength: The break-in note is right in the above-the-fold bullets, and the 'What to know before you buy' paragraph handles the cash and coin trade-offs honestly and in our calm voice.
mistake: It assumes the hidden pocket adds an extra note on top of the 10. That risks overstating cash capacity, which is the exact return reason we're fighting. The SEO title also runs slightly past 60 characters.
to10: Treat 10 notes as the total. Put the break-in note in the line under the button. Trim the SEO title. Add inches for US buyers and a way to measure whether returns drop.

strength: It treats 10 notes as the conservative total and adds inches for US buyers. It uses Tom's own 'brick in your back pocket' line, and it gives a measurement plan with correct return math (3.3 and 1.0 per 100 orders) plus a guardrail.
mistake: The break-in expectation never reaches the above-the-fold bullets or the line under the button. It also invents a '10 to 11 mm' figure for 6 to 7 cards that our data doesn't state.
to10: Add 'snug for the first week, then it settles' to a bullet or the line under the button. Drop the interpolated thickness. Confirm the word count stays under 1,000.

strength: Calm, readable copy in our voice. It answers the sunscreen white-cast and stickiness fears directly, and the Email 2 quiz branches point each person to one product.
mistake: Email 5 gives everyone the same routine: salicylic wash twice a day plus niacinamide. That is too much for nervous beginners and the dark-spot majority, and it undoes the quiz personalisation. It is also called '3-step' but shows two steps each morning and night.
to10: Branch Email 5 by quiz answer (niacinamide plus sunscreen for uneven tone). Personalise from Email 1. Add a holdout test and a projection of what a lift is worth.

strength: Data drives the whole series. It shows sales per click, gives the matched product from Email 1, and builds per-concern routines in the code-reminder email. It adds sensible Klaviyo settings (entry filter, cart pause, exit) plus a holdout test with correct ₹ projections.
mistake: Some emails read like spec sheets, with no greeting or sign-off, and prices like ₹628.20 look clumsy. Email 4 sends people back to comparing all three products, which works against the 'one product' message.
to10: Round prices to whole rupees and add a warm greeting and sign-off to each email. Make Email 4's CTA point to the matched product rather than all three.

strength: Diagnoses the real reasons people left: the retired blend and late deliveries. Pairs that with clean, checkable profit maths (₹557 and ₹442), a cost line for discounts given to people who would have bought anyway, and the delivery gate for ex-subscribers.
mistake: Puts the 46 to 90 day 'slipping' group behind the 91 to 180 day group. It handles them only with a side note about a day-28 nudge, never sizes or values them, and its profit figure rests on an optimistic two orders per returner.
to10: Make the 9,000 at-risk buyers wave 1 and value them in the profit table. Show a break-even lift per group. Give a conservative profit range alongside the optimistic one.

strength: Gets the order right: slipping buyers first with no discount, then Monsoon Dark, older groups after that, and ex-subscribers only once the delivery gate is met. It adds a conservative email-only profit range, real launch dates and compliance details, plus a smart Monsoon Dark pre-order idea.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark email asks for a quiz instead of naming the closest roast we still sell. The ex-subscriber email does not prove delivery is fixed with an on-time figure and does not name the farm or roast. Offering 15% off to the coldest 365+ group is questionable.
to10: Name the matched roast in the Monsoon Dark email and put the on-time rate and the farm in the subscriber email. Include break-even lift per group, and explain where the ₹535 per ex-subscriber figure comes from.

strength: A clean diagnosis that separates what is proved from what needs checking. The math is right: $71 contribution against $104 to acquire, a $79 counterfactual if Meta had held, $94 18-month value, and 1.8 points of linen returns. It ties directly to clear owners, first steps and a $94 cut rule.
mistake: The gross-profit impact of each move is mostly qualitative ('High', 'Medium'), so the ranking is asserted rather than sized. The flow-revenue target is left as a vague 'pre-January level'.
to10: Put a dollar or margin-point estimate on each move so the ranking is shown, not just claimed. Set a concrete flow-revenue target. State the overall return-rate shift (5.2% to 7.0%).

strength: It sizes every move in contribution points with low, likely and high ranges, sets decision lines at weeks 4 and 8, and derives a contribution baseline. It also catches the brand risk that the 'nice hotel' quote reads as a hotel-quality claim, and adds a smart swatch-kit test.
mistake: It is dense and hard to read for a grade-8 brand. It invents dates and a Black Friday timeline. It leans on derived figures (7.8%/13.6%) and an unsourced 'practitioner yardstick'. It also leaves flow revenue off the scorecard.
to10: Simplify the language and the working. Drop the invented calendar or state it as an assumption. Add flow revenue to the scorecard. Show more plainly why linen ranks fifth when it sits at the root of the Meta problem.

strength: It ties the threshold decision to COD refusals and keeps ₹499 because that is where refusals drop from 29% to 17%. It adds a one-click ₹199 lip balm in the cart for orders under ₹499 and offers a COD fee as a separate test. The maths checks out: 2,320 orders sit in the ₹499–598 band, about 800 refused COD orders a month cost about ₹1.04 lakh, and the Glow Routine earns ₹537 gross profit.
mistake: It is dense and heavy on numbers, with lakh ranges everywhere, so it is hard to scan. The copy is only adequate, not very cheerful.
to10: A cleaner layout, warmer and more on-brand bundle copy, and a one-line summary of the margin per order for each threshold option.

strength: Clear bundle ladder on the serum page with friendly copy that fits Kavya and Ishita. It makes a good case against a discounted ₹849 duo and judges results on profit per visitor.
mistake: It assumes only 6% of orders fall between ₹499 and ₹598. The data implies about 13.5% (around 2,300 orders), so the ₹599 case understates the risk. It misses that shampoo plus lip balm (₹598) falls short of ₹599. It does not use COD/RTO in the threshold choice, and two of its three bundles both lean on the serum, with no second category beyond hair.
to10: Fix the size of the ₹499–598 band and redo the threshold maths. Build COD refusal cost into the threshold decision, perhaps with a COD-specific rule. Use the body duo instead of a second serum bundle.

strength: It leads with the in-app checkout bug and sizes it correctly (about 560 orders, ₹34 lakh margin a month). The sample-size maths fits our real traffic, and each test carries its own run dates and rupee value.
mistake: Firmness is the second biggest chat topic, but it is only handled inside review tabs. Some lines are hard to follow, such as the note on reading tests 1 and 2 in their four combined groups.
to10: Add a dedicated plain-words firmness test in our voice. Explain the two-lane interaction check more clearly.

strength: The funnel table breaks out the in-app browsers. It ties the 4,130 in-app pop-up errors to the 4,800 lost in-app carts, which makes the bug case convincing. It also adds an A/A test after the fix and a proper firmness test with no medical claims.
mistake: Test 5 bundles the hero image and the reviews move into one variant, so a win cannot be credited to either change. It also gives no rupee value for each test.
to10: Split the image change and the reviews move into separate tests, or ship the reviews move. Add the money each test's smallest detectable lift is worth.

strength: A clean, submittable template set with a sensible tiered confirm-or-hold flow. It also has practical ops ideas: quiet hours, a holdout, and moving one agent to a 2 pm to midnight shift to cover the evening chat wave.
mistake: The prepaid nudge has no incentive and is not tiered, so Tier 3 gets the same soft ask as metros. Labelling a pay-online nudge as Utility risks Meta recategorising it.
to10: Add a tiered prepaid incentive or COD advance for Tier 3, backed by the per-tier loss math. Use bolder Snitch voice in the scripts. Add a net-savings metric to the scorecard.

strength: Ties every tier decision to money: expected RTO loss per order is ₹70, ₹41 and ₹27, the ₹40 and ₹20 discounts sit below that loss, and calls go only to Tier 3 because only 4 agents carry chat. It adds holdouts, a net-saving metric and a tested ₹99 advance option.
mistake: T1 states an expected delivery date in the confirmation, which edges toward the date promises I want to avoid. It also misses fixing the 8 pm to midnight staffing gap with a shift change.
to10: Drop the date from T1. Add an evening agent shift. Give the scripts and templates a bit more Snitch punch.

strength: Plain, readable verdicts with rupee reasons. Relaunches the paused creator video first, splits out women 25 to 34, and cuts the Starter Kit on its ₹271 value. The budget adds to ₹5,60,000, and there is a creative section in Rohan's and Ananya's words.
mistake: The two-line system (safe ₹282 and break-even ₹394) makes verdicts fuzzy, and it still judges mainly on Meta's count. It scales Catalog DPA at frequency 5.2 and says Retargeting is probably over-counted, yet keeps it as a hold. Some numbers, such as the Gift Sets break-even and 'still lose ₹20,000', are not shown.
to10: One break-even per ad set on Shopify-adjusted, after-RTO numbers. Say what the plan does to total cost per purchase. Give a real fix for the Starter Kit, such as a prepaid-only offer, COD confirmation or pincode blocks, instead of only cutting it. Trim it to the word limit.

strength: Judges each ad set on its own after-RTO, attribution-adjusted break-even, so there is one honest line per ad set. Shows store-count profit by ad set and projects the outcome of the plan. Revives the creator video as a first move, narrows women to 25 to 34 and cuts the Starter Kit. The reserve is released by rule and the budget adds to ₹5,60,000.
mistake: Dense and a little cold, with less creative direction. Retargeting is labelled 'cut' but still gets ₹28,000. The UGC test gets ₹56,000 after only 5 days of data. Holding ASC flat when it is the main lever feels timid. The geo holdout test adds something to read when the owner asked for decisions.
to10: Label Retargeting 'trim', not 'cut'. Give the Starter Kit a concrete prepaid or COD-confirmation fix. Put the ASC relaunch up front with a few ad cuts and the exact scale steps. Simplify the table and add a short block of ad ideas in brand voice.

strength: The numbers table and day-30 rule come straight from the money. The 90-day break-even is $38.46 and the first-order break-even is $27.10. It reads the day-30 result three ways (store tags, survey, blended lift), which guards against inflated platform ROAS. It also adds an optional holdout.
mistake: It is dense and a bit over-engineered, with many thresholds that a small team has to track. The $4,750 return to Meta and the $1,625 steps are fiddly. Day 1 to 3 spends nothing and the first 12 ads are partly new shoots that are not made yet. The hook table is mostly the creator's words rather than ad scripts.
to10: Simplify the thresholds into a one-page daily checklist. Give a firmer plan for the 8 staff videos and creator fees. Add a short script or caption for the top 3 hooks. Be explicit that the March licence end falls inside or after the 30 days.

strength: It is very Monday-ready. It has a clean set-up checklist, role owners, brand don't-say rules, a price-handling note and a Scale campaign that reuses post IDs. Clear pass/hold/fail scorecard.
mistake: Day-30 pass is partly judged on TikTok-reported cost per first order, and its new-customer lift row is weaker than the first plan's. It treats $38 as a first-order target, but that only breaks even at 90 days. It says we lose about $11 on the first order, which is a fair framing, yet it then sets Month 2 at a 50% increase with little tie to the 90-day math. The 15-ads-in-5-concepts split is thin on the mission as the closing line, and the $1,000 reserve complicates the budget.
to10: Tie the pass/hold/fail more tightly to the 90-day break-even using survey or holdout data. Write the hooks in Maria's and Tasha's exact words. Drop the Smart+ option in month one. Note the timing of the March rights end against the 30 days.

strength: Production-ready detail on every concept: hook, scene timings, primary text, headline, size rules and a table of awareness and test. The first-three pick is tied to the data, and the test budget is sized as 15 purchases per concept. It also handles the dark-shell scuff and front-pocket issues.
mistake: It is dense and likely runs to or past the word limit. Some shoots, such as a real boarding gate or a plane aisle, are hard for a small team. 'Lifts it into a cab with one hand' hints at lightness beyond the specs.
to10: Trim to the word limit, offer cheaper shoot alternatives for the gate and aircraft scenes, and give each concept one explicit test variable and a clear success metric.

strength: Clean, scannable layout with the same fields for each concept. It adds the point that women bring 26% of purchases on 18% of spend, and concept 5 directly tests real travel scenes against the current flat colour shots. It also points concepts 6 and 7 at retargeting and the 41-plus group.
mistake: The test plan is thin. About ₹4,500 per concept is too little to judge, and one broad-targeting campaign blurs the audience-specific reads. Visuals and scene directions are lighter, so the team has more to fill in before shooting.
to10: Add scene-by-scene shot lists and headlines, raise the test budget to a meaningful level, and keep audiences separate so the women and men reads stay clean.

strength: Three distinct angles (blind test, 3 pm swap, game-day family) with clean timed shot tables, customer-language hooks, and no label-led opening. The 3 pm script answers the $3 price head-on.
mistake: Disclosure is only a caption '#ad' plus platform toggles, with no on-screen 'Ad' or spoken disclosure in the scripts. The test plan is thin, with no budget or kill thresholds. Little use is made of the cost-per-purchase data beyond the assumptions.
to10: Put disclosure into the scripts as on-screen text and a spoken line. Add a test plan with budget and cut thresholds from the $26/$32/$44 numbers. Include the approved claims list inside each creator brief. Confirm it fits under 1,300 words.

strength: Opens with a clear plan tied to the data: the label-read ads got the most spend ($24,000) at the worst $44 cost per purchase, so no ad opens on the label. Disclosure is built into every script ('Ad' on screen, spoken line, partnership toggles). A concrete test plan uses real numbers, such as $800 per ad and cutting hooks under a 19% view rate. The creator rules cover claims, banned words, deliverables and rights.
mistake: Some spoken lines are awkward ('It's linked right there', '12 afternoons for me'). '(if true)' tags inside hooks make them less ready to shoot. The creator rules and rights section push it past the word limit and add some clutter.
to10: Trim to under 1,300 words. Smooth the awkward lines and the '(if true)' hooks. Make each hook alternate change exactly one element. Put the three claims inside each individual creator brief so it can be sent as is.

strength: Clean, accurate set with all six angles distinct enough, the paused winner brought back in the first launch ad, taste tested against it, and price addressed directly, each ad testing one clear thing, plus backups.
mistake: Primary texts lean on '12 g protein. No added sugar.' as a tag, which makes several of them feel samey. Headline H1 pairs with P1 redundantly. Ad C vs A comparison muddles what is being tested. Relies on '1 in 4' rounding for 26%. Also assumes 27-char limits with no explanation for the stricter limit.
to10: Make each primary text fully distinct without repeating the protein/sugar tag, add Aditya and Priya's own phrases more vividly, and give a cleaner single-variable design for the four launch ads.

strength: Primary texts are truly different and written in the customers' own words (samosa, 'trained today', 'Fair. Here's your ₹90'), the price objection is handled head-on, and the launch plan comes with a test design, budget, kill rule and fatigue rule that make it executable tomorrow.
mistake: Invents a budget (₹6,000/day) and an elaborate test setup the owner did not ask for, with a minor arithmetic wobble (₹1,200 x 5 cells = ₹6,000, but the stated 14-day total and 'Day 14' read go well beyond the brief). Control ad is a fifth cell, so 'four combinations' is slightly stretched. Possibly near the word limit.
to10: Trim the extra experiment scaffolding and unstated budget assumptions, keep the strong copy, and state clearly that the ₹ figures are placeholders the owner can change.

strength: The cash number is stated plainly as about 10 notes laid flat, and it appears in the subtitle, bullets, spec table, FAQ and the line under the button. It also says the 10 is the total with the hidden pocket included, which is the safe choice for cutting cash returns. The measurement section ties it back to my numbers (3.3 returns per 100 orders on cash, about 1.0 early tight returns) and gives a fallback if conversion drops.
mistake: The break-in note is missing from the bullets and from the line under the add-to-cart button, even though that is where it would stop the early 'too tight' returns. It is also at the edge of the word limit because of the extra measurement section, and the '10 to 11 mm' figure for 6 to 7 cards is slightly extrapolated.
to10: Add 'snug for the first week, then it settles' to a bullet or the line under the button. Trim the measurement section to stay clearly under 1,000 words. Use the 142-of-400 review count as proof.

strength: It puts the break-in note in a bullet and in the description, FAQ and spec section, and uses the 142-of-400 review count as proof. The 'what you should know before you buy' paragraph is honest in a way that builds trust.
mistake: It invents a fact: the hidden pocket takes 'one more flat note'. That overstates capacity, which is what drives the 44% cash returns and what my brand notes forbid. Other unsupported details are 'parking meters' and 'so cards stay put'.
to10: Drop the invented hidden-pocket capacity and keep 10 notes as the total. Add the break-in note to the line under the button. Add a short plan for measuring the effect on returns and conversion.

strength: Polished, calm, on-brand emails with a clean timing table and exit rule. Email 4 answers the white cast, stickiness and makeup questions with the review line as proof. The slow-start rules in Email 3 are easy to follow.
mistake: Email 5 gives everyone the same 3-step routine, including the salicylic wash for the dark-spot majority. This cuts against its own 'one product at a time' advice and misses the simple sunscreen-plus-niacinamide routine for uneven tone. Email 1 is generic and the series only branches once.
to10: Carry the quiz answer through Emails 1, 3 and 5. Make the dark-spot routine (morning sunscreen, night niacinamide) the main route. Add a way to test whether the series beats today's single email. Check that the final length stays within 1,800 words.

strength: The quiz answer shapes the whole series, so each person sees one product that fits them. Email 5 gives dark-spot readers the niacinamide-plus-sunscreen routine I hoped for, and the maths is right (₹998 to ₹898.20, ₹698 to ₹628.20). Email 3 opens with Sneha's own words, 'Every sunscreen makes me look grey', which is a strong subject line.
mistake: The bodies are terse and carry no first-name greeting, so they read a little less warm than they could. The 'read the label' email is more generic than the others. The tests section may push the total past the word limit.
to10: Add a first-name greeting and a bit more warmth to the bodies. Make Email 4 do more for the dark-spot majority. Trim the tests section so the total stays within 1,800 words.

strength: It ranks the groups the way I would. The 46 to 90 day group goes first with no code, Monsoon Dark gets its own track, and ex-subscribers wait behind a delivery gate. Group sizes are netted for overlap, and the profit table is built on the holdout-adjusted contacted counts.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark draft promises a match but never names it or uses a farm or roast placeholder. The profit estimate also covers only first returning orders plus a loose 12-month extension, and a few details are odd, such as the ₹535 per ex-subscriber figure and a break-even lift given only for group G6.
to10: Name the closest dark roast in the Monsoon Dark draft and put a farm in every draft. Give a break-even lift for every group, not just G6. Show the 12-month value explicitly. Trim a little so it sits clearly inside the word limit.

strength: It is clean and easy to read. The drafts use farm and match placeholders. The delivery gate is sound, with a fix for each cancel reason. The profit maths checks out (₹557, ₹442, and a net of ₹8.5 lakh with low and high cases).
mistake: It starts with the 91 to 180 day group and gives the 9,000 customers at 46 to 90 days only an always-on nudge, not a campaign. Those are the cheapest customers to win back. It also gives group C 10% off from the first message, leading with price to a cold group.
to10: Make the 46 to 90 day group wave 1 with a reminder and no discount. Net the subscriber overlap out of group A. Add a break-even lift per group. Cover the Monsoon Dark buyers in the 91 to 180 band as a separate, sized track.

strength: It works out a real contribution-margin baseline (13.6% a year ago, 7.8% now) and sizes every move in points of margin, with the working shown. Each move has an owner, effort, week-4 and week-8 lines, and the scorecard carries action thresholds. This is what lets me rank by gross profit and effort.
mistake: It is dense, and probably over the 1,600-word cap. Some claims are unsupported, such as the 'practitioner yardstick' for flows. The gain sizes rest on stacked assumptions, and the 'week 2 line' shorthand is cryptic.
to10: Trim to the word limit and write the sizing in plainer words. Drop the unsourced benchmark. Give each move an explicit first-week step. Keep the 'proved' and 'to check' split and the baseline math.

strength: It is clear and well organised. It separates proved from still-to-check, with an owner and a date on each check. The $94 payback rule per ad set and the per-channel payback math (Meta loses $27, Google breaks even, other makes $14) are sharp. The stop list is practical and fits the brand.
mistake: It never computes the contribution-margin baseline, saying 'set baseline in week 1'. The impact of each move is mostly qualitative ('high', 'medium'), so the ranking by gross profit is weakly backed. The core-product return fixes are low value.
to10: Compute the contribution baseline and put a number on each move's gain. Add a first-week action per move. Give the scorecard action thresholds, and put the Meta reset and flows ahead of the minor returns fixes.

strength: It uses COD refusals in the decision. It adds a lip balm cart offer for orders under ₹499, proposes a ₹49 COD fee, and works out break-even for each bundle. It also gives a full test plan with stop rules and guardrails.
mistake: It is dense and a bit over the word limit. The 'bad news' block and the many projection ranges make it hard to skim. It also keeps the ₹499 threshold with only a weak case, so the main money question ends in 'test it'.
to10: Trim it to the word limit and state the threshold call more firmly, with one clear recommended number and a simpler money table. Spell out the ₹500 to 699 band maths at the top. Make the lip balm cart add-on a named fourth item instead of a side note.

strength: It is clean and easy to read. The bundle ladder on the serum page is a good idea. It also commits to a clear threshold (₹599) and shows a simple outcome table.
mistake: The threshold maths rests on an invented guess that only 6% of orders sit between ₹499 and ₹598. That gives a gain of only about ₹28k a month. It also barely uses COD and RTO for small orders, and it never considers a COD fee or a prepaid-only rule.
to10: Replace the 6% guess with a figure drawn from the order bands, and build COD refusal cost into the threshold decision. Make the three bundles three different jobs by dropping the overlapping Serum + Lip Balm bundle for a body or add-on bundle. Add a cart add-on to cross the threshold.

strength: It puts the in-app checkout fix first and sizes it in rupees. It then gives sample-size maths that checks out against my traffic. Add to cart is the main metric for the page-layout tests, and orders per session is kept for the tests that need it. It also catches that add to cart can mislead on the delivery and EMI tests.
mistake: It is well over the 1,500-word limit and dense. It adds a 'bolder move' nobody asked for and assumes calendar dates. Ranks 2 to 4 are barely justified, and firmness is only covered indirectly through the reviews tabs.
to10: Cut it to 1,500 words and drop the bolder-move section. Add one line on why each test sits at its rank. Show the funnel table by browser at the top. Add plain-words firmness copy.

strength: The opening funnel table splits the data by device and browser, with correct rates. It spots the in-app checkout bug and sizes it correctly at about 560 orders and ₹34 lakh a month, flagged as a ceiling. The A/A test, the in-app cookie warning and the 11-week schedule are practical touches.
mistake: Test 5 bundles a new hero image with a reviews move, so a result cannot be attributed. Orders per session is the main metric for the size test, which forces a 4-week run and a 12% minimum detectable lift. The firmness test depends on a placeholder rating and sits above the reviews idea, and the 11-week schedule is slow.
to10: Split test 5 into two tests. Use add to cart or checkout reach as the main metric where it fits. Show the rupee value of each test, and say plainly that small lifts will not be detectable at this conversion rate. Stay inside the word limit.

strength: Complete and careful. Ten templates with sample values, clear flow steps, a night auto-reply plus a shift move for the 31% after-hours wave, and sensible compliance guardrails such as quiet hours, message caps and a 10% holdout.
mistake: The prepaid nudge is one flow for everyone with no incentive, and it is filed as Utility, which Meta may recategorise. Pincode risk only changes what happens after no reply, not the nudge itself. The cart sizing assumes about 18,000 abandoned carts a month, a figure the brief never gives.
to10: Tier the prepaid nudge and its incentive by pincode risk, file the nudge as Marketing, and show the RTO loss per COD order by tier. Drop the invented cart volume, and keep the 7-day exchange policy flagged as a placeholder.

strength: Targets by pincode risk. It puts Tier 3 first, with calls and a 48-hour cancel, and works out expected loss per COD order (₹70, ₹41, ₹27) to size the ₹20 and ₹40 prepaid incentives. T4 is correctly Marketing. It also adds holdouts, a net-saving metric and an honest 'bad news' note.
mistake: The ₹20 and ₹40 discounts and the ₹99 advance are invented numbers, and auto-cancelling unconfirmed Tier 3 orders is aggressive. There is no shift change to staff the evening wave, and the ₹99 advance may trigger the upfront-payment distrust it names.
to10: Flag the discount amounts clearly as test values, add a softer path before the Tier 3 auto-cancel, and say how agent hours move to cover the evening. Trim the tables so the templates are easier to copy into the provider.

strength: It judges every ad set on store-adjusted, after-refusal profit and forecasts the result. It also adds a clever state-split test that checks whether retargeting pays at all.
mistake: The 86% prospecting attribution is an invented midpoint, and it drives every break-even figure. Retargeting is labelled 'Cut' but is only halved. Committing only ₹4.1 lakh leaves growth on the table even though the warehouse can ship more.
to10: Explain the attribution split more plainly, label calls consistently, add 2 or 3 new cuts of the 'Dad's razor' hook, and include a short creative brief in our voice.

strength: The 'safe line versus break-even line' idea is easy to act on. The budget table adds up, the ASC scale-up ladder has clear gates, and there is a creative section in our customers' own words, including new cuts of the 'Dad's razor' hook.
mistake: The ad set table shows profit on Meta's own count, which makes ASC and retargeting look profitable when on real orders they likely are not. It also keeps retargeting at ₹40,000 despite 6.8 frequency.
to10: Show each ad set's result on store-matched orders as well, trim retargeting harder or test whether it adds sales at all, and give a forecast of the 14-day outcome.

strength: Every rule is tied to our own numbers. It sets the $38.46 90-day break-even and $57 stop line, gives a budget that adds to exactly $30,000, and writes hooks in Maria's and Tasha's own words. It also catches that our trend sound isn't cleared for ads, and it proposes a state holdout for a cleaner day-30 read.
mistake: It is dense and table-heavy for a Monday handoff. It leans on 8 staff phone videos where the main bet should be briefing more on-feet worker creators. One of its three day-20 release reads is TikTok-reported cost.
to10: Add a short creator brief for 6 to 10 new on-feet workers, name an owner for each workstream beyond set-up, and trim the tables so the team can scan it quickly.

strength: It reads cleanly and the team could run it as written. It has a thorough set-up list (event dedupe, domain verification, comment moderation), names an owner for each task, handles price without leading with a discount, and plans to own rights to winners before the March licences end. The day-30 scorecard includes an incrementality check.
mistake: The hooks are less directly in our customers' words. Concept 4's close-ups drift toward product shots. A $76 no-purchase kill is aggressive for a $62 AOV, and it misses that the trend sound isn't cleared for ads.
to10: Write the hooks in Maria's exact phrases and add a holdout or survey-based read to the pass/fail table. Also justify the $34 scale threshold and the $45 fail line against the 90-day break-even.

strength: Every concept states a clear test question tied to the right cost per purchase. The first-three pick covers belt-skip, women solo travellers and quiet wheels, and the numbers check out (26% of purchases, ₹292 a trip, ₹1,515 blended).
mistake: Judging each concept after only about ₹4,500 of spend, or three purchases, is too little to tell a winner from luck. There are also no headlines and no scene timing, so the creative team still has gaps to fill.
to10: Set a more realistic test budget per concept. Add headlines and second-by-second scene notes. Give a little more insight beyond the data I already have, such as handling the front-pocket complaint.

strength: It is close to production-ready: safe zones, sizes, scene timings, headlines with character counts and a sensible 15-purchase test budget per concept. It also handles the scuff and front-pocket problems up front and opens with the three to make first.
mistake: Primary texts run a bit long and spec-listy for our short-line, grade-7 voice. 'What it tests' gets only one line each in the table, and calling weekend couples 'unaware' is questionable.
to10: Trim the primary texts to short, calm lines. Give each concept a fuller, single-variable test statement next to its creative.

strength: It is tied tightly to my numbers. It opens on taste because taste tests cost $26 a purchase, keeps the label out of every opening, puts price on screen in every script, and includes a costed test plan with cut-off rules, plus rights and deliverables for the creators.
mistake: The script tables are cluttered. 'Olipop paid me' sits in the middle of spoken lines, and '(if true)' notes appear in the dialogue, so the scripts read stiffer and less playful than our voice. It also runs close to the word limit.
to10: Make the spoken lines warmer and more natural. Keep the disclosure in the brief and the label rather than in awkward dialogue. Trim to stay well under 1,300 words.

strength: It sounds like us. 'Still fizzy. Still sweet. Still my treat.' is on brand. The briefs are clean and easy for a creator to follow, and the disclosure and claim rules are clear.
mistake: Price is only answered out loud in one script. The test plan is thin, with no budget or decision thresholds. Some alternate hooks change the whole format instead of one thing, so I can't learn much from testing them.
to10: Add a budget, kill and scale thresholds, and the reasoning from my data. Handle the $3-a-can objection in each angle. Make each alternate hook change only one element.

strength: It brings back the paused front-of-pack winner in fresh words, tests taste and price head-on, and builds a full run plan. That plan has a control, a budget that matches my past spend, early-cut and fatigue rules, and correct purchase math.
mistake: The launch set skips the 4 pm snack and texture angles. The plan is dense for a non-expert owner to run without help.
to10: Add an image or creative note for each angle, plus a plainer one-line summary of what to do on day 14.

strength: The diagnosis of the past ads is clear and correct. It also adds a useful backup plan in case review quotes aren't allowed.
mistake: The primary texts overlap a lot. Two are front-of-pack, two are taste/texture, and most end on '12 g protein. No added sugar.' That is the sameness I wanted to avoid. Half the launch set also goes to the transparency angle.
to10: Make all six texts truly different angles, including a clean 4 pm snack line. Cut the repeated spec tail. Add a control ad and a budget plan for the test.

strength: It is open about trade-offs across the whole page. Break-in sits in a bullet, the description, the 'what fits' section and the FAQ. The 'What to know before you buy' paragraph sounds just like us and should cut returns.
mistake: It guesses that the hidden pocket takes one extra note beyond the 10. That risks overstating cash, which is the exact problem behind 44% of returns. It is flagged as an assumption, but it still appears in the copy.
to10: Treat 'about 10 notes' as the total. Add inches for US buyers like Tom. Put the break-in note in the line under the add-to-cart button. Add a short plan for checking whether returns actually drop.

strength: The cash figure is conservative: about 10 notes in total, hidden pocket included. It gives inches for US buyers and uses Tom's 'brick in my back pocket' line. It also adds a way to measure success, with return rates per 100 orders worked out correctly, a conversion-rate guardrail and a fallback plan.
mistake: Break-in is not in the bullets above the fold or in the line under the add-to-cart button, where it would stop more of the early 'too tight' returns. The 10–11 mm figure for 6–7 cards is an estimate, not from the data.
to10: Put 'Snug for the first week, then it settles' in a bullet or under the add-to-cart button. Drop the estimated 10–11 mm figure or mark it as an estimate.

strength: It is built tightly on my data. The quiz answer drives which product people see, and the sunscreen email answers the white cast and stickiness worries. It also covers exit, cart-pause and holdout rules and works out what a lift is worth in rupees.
mistake: Some lines don't fit every product. The WhatsApp says 'every other night' even when the matched product is sunscreen. Email 4 puts all three products back in front of people, which undoes the one-product focus. Subject lines rarely name the active and its strength.
to10: Name the active and strength in more subject lines. Tailor the WhatsApp usage line to each product. Keep Email 4 focused on one matched product. Add a short tingling-versus-irritation note to the start-slow email.

strength: The copy is warm and on-brand. The branched Email 2 has subject lines that name the active and strength. The labelling explanation and the tingling-versus-burning advice are helpful.
mistake: Email 5 pushes the full 3-product routine (₹1,297) to everyone. That includes salicylic wash twice a day for dry or sensitive people who were told not to start with acids, so it contradicts Email 2 Version C and the one-idea, start-slow rule. The sunscreen email also comes later than it should, and the whole thing likely runs past my word limit.
to10: Make Email 5 branch by skin concern with a 1–2 product routine. Move the sunscreen-doubts email earlier. Tighten the copy to fit 1,800 words. Add a holdout test and a cart-flow pause.

strength: Fix-the-reason-first logic runs all the way through. The Monsoon Dark email names the blend and the roasters' closest match, and the subscriber email holds back until on-time delivery is proven, then leads with picking your own date.
mistake: It ranks the 91 to 180 day group first. The 9,000 customers at 46 to 90 days, who are the cheapest to win back, appear only as a side 'day-28 nudge' and are left out of the ranked plan and the value table.
to10: Make 46 to 90 days wave 1 with no discount. State the minimum lift each group needs to break even, not only the lift that would be detectable. Show the value calculation per group more simply.

strength: Right order and right discipline. The slipping 46 to 90 day group goes first with no code, discounts rise with lapse age and never pass 15%, there is a delivery gate for ex-subscribers, and the measurement plan is solid: holdout, profit read from order data, and keep/drop rules per group. It also adds a bold, testable Monsoon Dark pre-order idea.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark email sends people to a quiz instead of naming the closest match. A few numbers are loose: the ₹535 figure for ex-subscribers is unexplained, the cold brew date jumps to 2027, and every G2 returner is valued at the 10%-off profit even though steps 1 and 2 carry no discount.
to10: Name the closest dark roast and its farm in the Monsoon Dark email, with the quiz as the fallback. Tidy the per-group profit figures. Add the break-even lift per group.

strength: It turns the diagnosis into hard numbers I can manage to. It estimates contribution after ads at 7.8% now, down from 13.6%. Each move is sized in margin points, with an owner, week-4 and week-8 checkpoints, and clear 'continue, change or stop' rules. It also caps ad sets at the $94 payback level.
mistake: It is dense and full of jargon ('points', solving for w, low/likely/high ranges), so it is hard for me to read quickly or share with the team. Some figures look more precise than the stacked assumptions allow. The 'flows should be about half of email revenue' yardstick is stated without support.
to10: Rewrite it in plainer, grade-8 language and add a short week-by-week timeline. Show the linen return impact on the overall return rate (about 5.2% to 7.0%). Give the flow target as the pre-January figure rather than an outside benchmark.

strength: It reads clearly and is easy to follow. The 'needs checking' table gives each question an owner and a deadline. The payback by channel stands out: Meta loses $27 per customer, Google breaks even, and other channels make $14. It also has a simple 90-day timeline and sensible return fixes across the whole range.
mistake: The scorecard does not commit to a contribution baseline ('set in week 1', target 'up every month') and has no action thresholds. The moves are ranked by words like 'High' and 'Medium' instead of sized gains, so I cannot compare them properly.
to10: Estimate the current contribution margin and give it a day-90 number. Size each move in dollars or margin points. Add trigger thresholds to each scorecard line so the weekly meeting leads to decisions.

strength: It puts COD refusals at the centre of the threshold decision. It shows that ₹499 already sits on the line where refusals drop from 29% to 17%, and it costs the leak correctly at about ₹1.04 lakh a month (6,880 orders under ₹499, 40% COD, 29% refused, ₹130 each). It also adds a COD fee option and a lip balm cart add-on to plug that leak.
mistake: The opening 'bad news' block crams in break-even counts and lakh ranges before I know what the bundles are, so it is hard to follow on a first read. The face wash + serum pair is only offered as a three-item set, with no plain duo.
to10: Explain the bundles first, then the money, in plainer words. Put each bundle's profit and break-even next to its name. Make the bundle copy warmer and more playful, closer to Plum's cheerful voice.

strength: The price ladder on the serum page (₹599, then ₹749, then ₹999) is easy to grasp and suits both Ishita and Kavya. The bundle copy is friendly and the reasoning reads clearly.
mistake: The case for moving to ₹599 rests on assuming only 6% of orders fall between ₹499 and ₹598. My data puts 27% of orders in the ₹500 to 699 band, so that slice is more likely 12 to 14%, and the profit figure may be off. It also mostly ignores COD refusals in the threshold decision. Two of the three bundles hang on the serum, with no second category beyond hair.
to10: Base the threshold maths on the real order bands. Count refusal costs by order value and treat COD orders separately, for example with a COD fee or a higher bar for COD. Spread the bundles across categories, with body as a real option.

strength: It puts the in-app checkout bug first and sizes it at ₹17 to 34 lakh a month. It also gives sample-size maths that match the traffic, and it explains why add to cart would mislead for the delivery and EMI tests.
mistake: It is dense and full of jargon. Phrases like 'server-side split so the old page never flashes' and 'read in four combined groups' are hard for me to follow, and the calendar dates are invented without being flagged as assumptions.
to10: Use plainer language and a simple funnel table so I can see the browser split myself. Label the dates as assumptions, and add a plain-words firmness change for the 'too soft' worry.

strength: The funnel table by browser makes the checkout bug obvious at a glance. The fix is sized correctly at about 560 orders and ₹34 lakh margin a month, and the schedule, A/A check and assumptions section are clear.
mistake: Test 5 bundles the hero image with moving the reviews, so if it wins I won't know which change did it. The firmness test rests on an assumed problem ('foam terms') that is not in my page notes.
to10: Split the bundled test 5. Give a number in each hypothesis, and add the point that add to cart can mislead when the date or EMI is shown on the page.

strength: Very practical, complete flows. The tier 3 48-hour hold, the switch from COD to UPI sent as a normal chat right after confirmation, and moving one agent to a 2 pm to midnight shift all fit how we actually run.
mistake: The prepaid nudge (template 3) is filed as Utility. Meta will likely recategorise it, and I wanted that nudge as Marketing. Tier 3 also gets no stronger nudge or incentive, and the 7-day exchange window is made up.
to10: File the prepaid nudge as Marketing with a tiered incentive. Make the tier 3 handling stronger, for example an advance option. Show net savings after costs. Pull the exchange wording from our real policy instead of assuming it.

strength: It sizes the prepaid discount by pincode tier using the expected RTO loss (₹70, ₹41 and ₹27 per order). It also has holdouts, a net-saving metric, a ₹99 tier 3 advance test, and skips confirmation for trusted repeat buyers like Arjun. That shows me where the money actually is.
mistake: Promising agent calls to all unconfirmed tier 3 orders could stretch 4 agents thin. The T1 confirmation also shows a delivery range before the order ships, which edges toward promising dates.
to10: Use an automated call or IVR for tier 3 confirmations. Drop the EDD from T1. Add an evening agent shift so after-hours size questions get a person.

strength: Every ad set gets a verdict with a rupee reason, and the budget adds to ₹5,60,000. It relaunches 'Dad's razor vs mine' first and puts a rupee value on pausing it (about ₹65,000). It narrows women's razors to 25 to 34 instead of killing them, cuts the Starter Kit as a COD trap, and ends with concrete creative direction in Rohan's and Ananya's words.
mistake: The two-line system (safe ₹282 and break-even ₹394) makes some calls feel hedged, such as 'Fix, then scale' and the 'hold' labels. The Meta-count loss figure (₹29,000) does not quite reconcile. It also adds an unrequested ₹35,000 'new creative test' line and probably runs over the word limit.
to10: Pick one clear Shopify-adjusted break-even per ad set and give one flat verdict each. Tighten the length, make the loss math reconcile, and open with the relaunch as a literal Monday first step.

strength: It is the most rigorous on real economics. Break-even is worked out per ad set from its own COD and RTO mix with a haircut for Meta over-counting. It also catches the paused creator video, the 25 to 34 split and the Starter Kit trap, and the release rules for the reserve are specific.
mistake: It scales nothing and parks ₹1,49,100 in a reserve, so the owner still has to decide what to do with a quarter of the budget. Retargeting is labelled 'Cut' but still gets ₹28,000. The UGC test is raised on only 31 purchases. The geo-holdout 'bolder move' adds complexity when the owner asked for decisions, not more measurement. Invented dates (14 to 27 November) are not in the brief.
to10: Commit the reserve to ASC with the relaunched creator video as the clear first move. Make the verdict labels match the budget actions, drop the holdout experiment, remove the invented dates, and add a short creative section that speaks in Rohan's and Ananya's voice.

strength: The money logic runs through the whole plan. The $27.10 first-order and $38.46 90-day break-even numbers set the target, the stop line and the kill spend. Day 30 is judged on three reads (store tags, survey, blended lift) plus a holdout, not platform ROAS. The budget adds to exactly $30,000, and the hooks are written in Maria's and Tasha's own words.
mistake: The kill and scale rules overlap and come in many small variants ($100, $114, $190, a 3-day window, a 7-day window), so the team has to work to read them. It also assumes new 'Clogs test' and 'Hour ten' posts from the same two creators, which we have not agreed. The dense tables are not grade 6-7 reading.
to10: Collapse the kill rules into one short ladder. Spell out the brand guardrails (banned words, giving line) for the creative team. Add a short owner list for Monday. Flag the new creator posts as an assumption that needs a yes from the creators.

strength: It is very easy to hand to a team. It has a clear week-0 checklist, a list of what never to say, a way to answer price inside the ad, a plan to own the rights before the March licences end, and named owners. The day-30 scorecard has pass, hold and fail columns, plus a check on whether TikTok adds new customers or just takes credit for Meta's.
mistake: The day-30 bar is not fully consistent. It asks for 790 or more first orders (30,000 / 38), but only $29,000 is planned spend, and the first 14 days are excluded from the cost judgment. The 90-day repeat value sets the $38 target but does not drive the final decision, and there is no holdout. Some hooks are generic, for example concept 5 just repeats concept 1.
to10: Make the order-count threshold match the spend actually planned. Tie the month-2 decision more clearly to 90-day payback with survey and holdout checks. Write sharper hooks in Maria's own words, such as 'My feet don't ache by hour ten.'

strength: It reads like a production brief. Each concept has timed scenes, a headline with character count, and a sound-honesty note. The three picks follow the data (women's cost per purchase, work flyers, quiet wheels). It also sets a test budget with a clear win and stop rule, and keeps claims strictly to the approved specs.
mistake: The concept details are uneven, and the "who and awareness" and "tests" fields sit in a table instead of under each concept. Concepts 2 and 7 are both proof-led and feel close. The "lifts it into a cab with one hand" shot hints at lightness beyond the approved spec.
to10: Put awareness and test variable under every concept. Swap one proof-led concept for a bolder idea. Drop the one-hand lift. Tighten the primary text into shorter, calmer lines in our voice.

strength: It follows my requested structure for every concept: angle, who and awareness, hook, format, visual, text, test. The primary text is short and calm in our voice. It reads the data well (26% of purchases from 18% of spend). The reviews carousel and the plan to keep a control ad running are useful.
mistake: Test spend is thin: about ₹4,500 per concept gives little to judge on. Broad targeting would blur the women-versus-men read it wants. The gate concept shows cabin dimensions that are not in the approved specs. It ignores the front-pocket request. Some copy leans on "quiet" and "smooth" as our own claims rather than review quotes.
to10: Add headlines and exact specs per format. Set a real test budget and audience split per concept. Keep quiet, smooth and sharp strictly as quoted review lines. Add a note on the front-pocket objection.

strength: It reads the spend data well (label reads got the most money and the worst results), answers the $3 price objection on camera with the '12 afternoons' idea, writes spoken and on-screen paid disclosure into each script, and adds a creator rights and delivery section plus a budgeted test plan.
mistake: It runs well over the 1,300-word limit and is dense. A few lines are clumsy, such as 'It's linked right there', and 'A new kind of soda' only closes one script.
to10: Cut it to 1,300 words by trimming the test plan and the bolder-move section. Close every ad on 'A new kind of soda', fix the awkward lines, and make the three hooks per script change exactly one thing.

strength: It is clean and fits the length limit. It keeps the brand voice throughout, ends every ad on 'A new kind of soda', and uses a natural 3 pm hook ('It's 3 pm. You know what that means.') and a candid price line.
mistake: The creator briefs are thin. They have no rights, deliverables or timing, and no spoken or on-screen disclosure beyond '#ad' and the partnership toggles. The test plan is generic, with no budget and no cut-off thresholds.
to10: Add deliverables, usage rights and deadlines to the briefs, plus an on-screen 'Ad' and a spoken disclosure line in each script. Add a test plan with a budget and kill thresholds based on the $26 and $32 benchmarks, and make the three scripts feel more distinct.

strength: The data read is accurate and tight. It brings back the paused winner as fatigue, leads with taste and the 9% price objection, and shows character counts and clean one-line tests.
mistake: Too many primary texts repeat '12 g protein. No added sugar.' P1 and P5 are the same angle, and P2 and P3 are both taste. The 4 pm snack angle is missing, and the voice is plainer than ours.
to10: Six truly different angles, with no repeated spec tail and a real 4 pm text. Add sharper, wittier lines in Aditya's and Priya's own words. Make each launch pair test one clear variable.

strength: Six distinct angles written in our blunt, witty voice and our customers' own words. 'Save yourself the flip', 'Fair. Here's your ₹90' and 'isn't a samosa' sound like us. The launch plan comes with a control, budget math, win rules and fatigue triggers.
mistake: It is dense and likely at or over the 1,000-word cap. The control cell and the 20% win rule add complexity we did not ask for. Ad D changes only the wording of the sugar ad, which is a weaker test than a new angle.
to10: Trim to safely under 1,000 words and cut some of the test mechanics. Make the fourth launch ad test a new idea, not a rewording. Show the 125-character limit more plainly for each primary text.

strength: Handles the cash and break-in issues in several places, and adds a measurement plan with the real return maths (3.3 per 100 orders, 1.0 per 100 early-tight returns) and a fallback if conversion drops. Assumptions are stated and cautious: the 10 notes is the total, hidden pocket included.
mistake: Says the sweet spot is 'about 10 to 11 mm' for 6 or 7 cards, which is an invented number. The line under the button leaves out the break-in note, which is the best place to cut early returns. The measurement section is extra and pushes the word count past the limit. Putting 'not a thick roll' in the subtitle area and bullets may scare a few buyers.
to10: Drop the invented 10 to 11 mm figure, put 'snug for the first week, then it settles' in the line under the button, trim to under 1,000 words, and keep the measurement plan as a short note.

strength: Puts the break-in note in the bullets above the fold, which targets the early 'too tight' returns, and states trade-offs plainly: 'We would rather tell you now than have you send it back.' The 'what fits' scenarios (light day, full day, most it takes) are easy to use.
mistake: Invents a fact: the hidden pocket takes 'one more flat note', so the total reaches about 11. That risks overstating cash capacity, which is the very problem we are trying to fix. It flags this as an assumption, but it still goes in the copy. It also says the wallet 'sits flat in a back pocket or jacket' without support, and 'slots are made snug so cards don't slide out' is a made-up reason. Nothing is said about how the work will be measured.
to10: Remove the invented extra note in the hidden pocket and the made-up reason for snug slots, put the break-in note under the button, and keep the cash number the same everywhere.

strength: Personalises the whole series by quiz answer, with a clear exit rule and a cart pause. It also adds a holdout test, uses the conversion numbers well, and puts the sunscreen fears into one email with the review quote as proof.
mistake: Email 2 mixes the slow-start plan with product blocks, which slightly breaks one idea per email. Email 1 also asks for a 14-day use before adding anything, which is slow. The sunscreen email puts the review quote ahead of any real fix for stickiness. A few figures, such as the projections, are extra and not asked for.
to10: Lean harder into the dark-spot routine of sunscreen plus niacinamide for the 44%, so the sunscreen is a morning step beside the serum. Tighten the emails so each carries one idea, trim the data commentary, and check the finish claims against the product page.

strength: Clean, readable, calm in voice, with three quiz-matched versions of Email 2 that each give how to start slowly. It answers 'I don't know which serum is for me' directly and the emails are short.
mistake: Email 5's 'full 3-step routine' puts the salicylic wash in the morning and at night, then a serum and sunscreen. That is more actives than a beginner needs, and it contradicts the one-at-a-time advice and the sensitive-skin path. It also uses 'help clear out oil' and 'help even out the look' claims that sit close to the line. The sunscreen email comes late at day 6.
to10: Build Email 5 as a routine matched to the quiz answer, with no double wash. Move the sunscreen answers earlier, add a cart pause and a holdout test, and tie the dark-spot path to sunscreen plus niacinamide.

strength: Complete and well costed. It has a gated ex-subscriber track, a no-discount start for Monsoon Dark buyers, and a worked profit table net of discounts and WhatsApp costs.
mistake: It puts the 91 to 180 day group first and treats the 9,000 customers at 46 to 90 days only as a future day-28 nudge. That is my cheapest group to win back, so it is not targeted now.
to10: Target the 46 to 90 day group first with a light reminder and no offer, and state the break-even lift per group. Make the drafts less generic and keep it clearly under 1,500 words.

strength: It gets the order right: slipping 46 to 90 day buyers first with no code, then Monsoon Dark buyers, with ex-subscribers held until delivery is fixed. It shows the 29% vs 6% Monsoon Dark gap, and its drafts use my own lines, such as "one coffee, not a list of 40" and Nisha's date-picking fix.
mistake: The pre-order idea for one more Monsoon Dark lot ignores that I stopped it for a reason. The "Stay or go" sunset email also sits close to guilt territory, and the ₹535 profit per returned subscriber is not explained.
to10: Drop or clearly caveat the Monsoon Dark pre-order. Soften the sunset wording and show the break-even lift per group. Add a few more finished drafts, such as G3 and G4.

strength: It quantifies every move in contribution-margin points, with a baseline (7.8% vs 13.6%), owners, week 4 and week 8 lines, and a scorecard that has action thresholds. It reads like a plan I could run on Monday.
mistake: It is dense, and some of its derived numbers (the 13.6% and 7.8% baselines, the gain sizings) rest on stacked assumptions. The 'worth at least $94' payback is also shaky. The 'Stop doing' item about site speed is a little odd. Some phrasing like 'Bad news' and the long working section is heavy for a grade-8 reader.
to10: Trim the working and the swatch-kit side idea. Keep the assumed baselines clearly labelled as estimates. Plainer prose with fewer formulas. Rank the moves explicitly by gross profit, not by gain divided by effort.

strength: It is clear and easy to read, and its checks table pairs each open question with an owner and a date. Per-channel payback is sharp (Meta loses $27 a customer, Google about breaks even, Other makes $14). It keeps to the brand: no sitewide sales, and the wash-test and swatch ideas speak to Sarah's fear.
mistake: Impact estimates are vaguer ('High', 'Medium') with few first-week steps and no gain figures in contribution terms. The scorecard has no contribution baseline ('set in week 1') and its targets are looser. It also puts the Meta reset below the linen pause, though Meta is the main cause.
to10: Put numbers on each move's gross profit and give a first-week step for each. Give a contribution baseline and week-by-week checkpoints. Rank the Meta reset first.

strength: It ties the threshold to the COD refusal problem and works out the money. It sizes the right slice of orders (about 2,320 between ₹499 and ₹598), proposes a lip balm cart add-on and a COD fee under ₹499, and gives a careful test plan with stop rules.
mistake: It is dense and likely runs over the 1,300-word limit. The 'bad news' section and the long projection ranges (−₹0.72 to +₹2.35 lakh) make it hard to act on, and the lakh figures rest on many assumptions.
to10: Cut it to 1,300 words and lead with one plain recommendation. Show the money in a short table, and write the page copy in a warmer, simpler voice.

strength: It is clear, within the length limit, and gives a clear recommendation. It uses Ishita's serum reorder to argue against ₹699, builds a simple price ladder on the serum page, and writes bundle copy in Plum's voice.
mistake: Its key assumption is wrong. It says orders between ₹499 and ₹598 are about 6% of orders, but the data points to roughly 13%. The money case for ₹599 is therefore thin, at about +₹28k a month. It also barely uses COD and RTO in the threshold decision.
to10: Size the ₹499 to ₹598 slice correctly from the spread. Make COD versus prepaid part of the threshold choice, add a body or other category bundle, and add a lip balm cart add-on.

strength: It puts the in-app checkout fix first with a hedged money range (₹17 to ₹34 lakh a month). Each test has sample sizes that match our traffic, a per-test money estimate, and a clear reason the hero image ranks last.
mistake: It is dense and jargon-heavy for a business owner ('server-side split', 'named segment', 'voids the result', the four-group note on tests 1 and 2). It also runs long and has a cold 'Bad news' tone. It has no test for firmness, our second most common chat question, and the bolder-move extra uses up words.
to10: The same rigorous maths in plain words, inside the word limit. Add a firmness and trial test with copy in our voice, drop the extras, and show the funnel by browser in one simple table up front.

strength: The funnel table by device and browser makes the in-app problem obvious. It links the 4,130 in-app pop-up errors to the 4,800 lost carts, sizes the fix at about 560 orders and ₹34 lakh a month, and recommends an A/A check. The tests cover delivery, sizes, firmness, EMI and COD, and the hero image and reviews.
mistake: Test 5 bundles the hero image and the reviews move, so a win cannot be traced to either change. The hypotheses carry no numbers. Running all five takes 11 weeks, which is slower than it needs to be, and the reviews move could simply ship.
to10: Split the hero and reviews into separate changes, with the reviews summary shipped now. State the detectable effect in orders and rupees for each test. Run the pairs in more parallel lanes to finish sooner, and give the exact delivery, trial and firmness copy in our voice.

strength: It treats Tier 3 as the main problem, with the RTO money worked out by pincode group. Tier 3 gets calls and a cancel rule, Tier 2 and Tier 3 get tiered prepaid discounts, and metros get a light touch. Holdouts and a net-saving check keep the flow honest.
mistake: The Tier 3 call load is thin for 4 agents who also handle chat. The 'bad news' bullet and the dense tables make it a little heavy to read. It also runs close to or over the word limit.
to10: Trim it to the word limit and say how the calls fit into agent hours. Add a plainer, more Snitch-sounding line to the reply scripts. Cut the Tier 3 discount and advance ideas down to one clear first test.

strength: It is clean and cautious, with clear assumptions, quiet hours, an evening agent shift for the after-hours wave, and a sensible weekly scorecard.
mistake: The prepaid nudge is one flow for everyone with no incentive, so Tier 3 is not targeted. The 'pay online' template is filed as Utility even though it is a promotional nudge, which risks recategorisation. Tier 3 only gets a call and a 48-hour hold.
to10: Make the prepaid nudge stronger and different by pincode band, with a Marketing template and a small incentive or advance for Tier 3. Show the RTO money by group. Put more Snitch bold voice into the templates and scripts.

strength: Every ad set is judged on an attribution-adjusted, after-RTO profit line, and the plan gives a dated first move for Saturday. The retargeting geo holdout is a smart way to test whether retargeting adds orders at all.
mistake: The 86%/72% attribution split is invented, and labels and numbers sometimes disagree: retargeting is marked 'Cut' but only halved. Committing just ₹4.1L of ₹5.6L, with zero scale calls, means it under-deploys budget even though stock and cash are fine.
to10: Fix the retargeting label. Justify or simplify the 86% assumption. Add a short creative brief for the revived hook. Give the reserve a clearer path to ASC so the team spends most of the budget when costs recover.

strength: The ₹282 safe line and ₹394 break-even line give the team a simple scale/hold/cut rule. It puts a rupee value of about ₹65k on the paused creator video. The women's age losses are broken out by band, and the creative brief uses Rohan's and Ananya's words. I checked the per-ad-set break-evens, profits and budget total, and they hold up.
mistake: The main results table is on Meta's count, so it shows ASC at +₹30k when the store-count view is far worse. Scaling Catalog DPA at frequency 5.2 is a stretch.
to10: Show a Shopify-adjusted profit column next to the Meta count. Hold Catalog DPA rather than scale it. Add a dated first-day checklist.

strength: Every rule comes from our own numbers. Break-even is $27.10 on the first order and $38.46 over 90 days, and the kill, learning and stop lines all derive from them. The budget sums exactly to $30,000. Hooks use Maria's and Tasha's actual words.
mistake: It is very dense with tables, so it reads like a spreadsheet for some of the team. The day-20 release rule also lets TikTok-reported cost count as one of its three votes.
to10: Add a short plain-language summary of who does what on Monday. Drop the platform-reported read from the release rule, or make it secondary to the store tags and survey.

strength: It is clean and easy to hand off. Set-up is thorough (dedupe, domain verification, comment moderation), the budget sums correctly with a reserve, and named owners are listed. It also plans to own rights before the March licences end.
mistake: The hooks lean less on our customers' own lines and leave out 'My feet don't ache by hour ten'. The day-30 order-count target of 790 assumes the full $30k is spent, even though $1k is a conditional reserve. The $76 no-purchase kill is aggressive for a new pixel.
to10: Write hooks directly from Maria's and Tasha's quotes. Align the day-30 order bar with actual spend. Add a geo holdout for a cleaner incrementality read.

strength: It is strict on claims and the numbers all check out. 'Quiet', 'light' and 'premium' appear only as buyers' review lines. The budget plan is checked: 15 purchases' worth per concept, about ₹63k in total, with a clear kill rule. The women's concept is ranked first, backed by the ₹1,058 vs ₹1,615 numbers.
mistake: Some primary text runs long and reads like a spec list, so it drifts from the short-line, grade 7 voice. Concepts 2, 6 and 8 are still fairly static-on-scene, closer to what we already run.
to10: Cut the primary text to short, punchy lines. Make one of the statics a more distinct format, such as a UGC or creator piece. Give each concept a single named test variable.

strength: The copy reads like our brand: short, calm lines such as 'Land. Roll. Leave.' The eight concepts are clearly spread across formats. Two touches are smart: concept 7 uses reviews to go after the costly 41+ group, and concept 5 is framed as a direct test of our current look. The math holds (26% of purchases, ₹292 a trip, +63 purchases).
mistake: Several lines put claims in our own voice that are not approved specs: 'No rattle', 'Quiet wheels' in the brand copy, 'rolls quiet'. Concept 2 puts product dimensions on screen, which are not on the approved list. The test budget of ~₹4,500 per concept is too thin to scale or cut on.
to10: Keep 'quiet' strictly to review quotes and drop the on-screen dimensions. Set a realistic test budget per concept. Lead the top three with the women's concept, since that is the cheapest proven audience.

strength: It ties every choice to my numbers: taste openers first, label reads only after the sip, price said on camera, and a test plan whose budget math checks out ($72k spend, $800 × 9 = $7,200, a cut-off at the 19% label-read rate). It also covers full creator terms: disclosure on both platforms, deliverables, safe zones, usage rights and timelines.
mistake: It's dense and close to the word limit. Some spoken lines are stiff, like 'Olipop paid me for this one' dropped in mid-taste-test. The price answer is weak ('12 afternoons for me'), and in Script 3 it's barely an answer at all.
to10: Give the price a real reason to pay, such as one good soda a day or less than an afternoon coffee-shop drink. Loosen the copy so it sounds warmer and more nostalgic, and trim it so creators can scan it fast.

strength: The voice is warm and playful and sounds like us. 'Still fizzy. Still sweet. Still my treat.' and the head-on '$3 a can? Yes. It's my one soda of the day' are the best price answer of the two. The creator briefs are clear and easy to read.
mistake: The test plan is thin, with no budgets, thresholds or kill rules. It is also weaker on creator deliverables and usage rights, and the alternate hooks change format, not just one variable. Script 1 and Script 3 barely address price.
to10: Add budget-per-ad and cut/scale thresholds based on the $26/$32/$44 numbers. Spell out deliverables, rights and timelines in the creator brief. Work the one-good-soda-a-day price line into at least two scripts.

strength: It is a complete plan I could launch tomorrow. It brings back the paused front-of-pack winner, leads with the taste angle and tackles the ₹90 price head-on. It adds a control cell, a budget whose maths checks out (₹16,800 a cell, about 58 purchases at ₹290), an early-cut rule and a fatigue rule.
mistake: Ad B pairs the taste text with the protein headline, so that test mixes two angles. It also slightly muddies how a win would be read.
to10: Make each launch combination test only one variable: pair taste with a taste or texture headline. Add one or two more witty lines in Aditya's voice, such as 'candy bars in gym clothes' without the dig at other brands.

strength: The diagnosis of the 90-day data is sharp. The A vs C test (front-of-pack fact vs 'you check the back') is clever, and the legal backup for the review quotes is a thoughtful extra.
mistake: Almost every primary text repeats '12 g protein. No added sugar.' This is exactly the sameness I warned against. Two of the six angles are also transparency, and the 4 pm snack angle is folded into the price line, so range suffers.
to10: Cut the repeated spec tail from each line and give the 4 pm snack its own text. Add a budget, a control and a stop rule so the test plan can actually run.

strength: It handles the trade-offs honestly and in the right place. The break-in note sits in an above-the-fold bullet. The page says plainly: 'If you often carry more than 10 notes... a larger wallet will serve you better.'
mistake: It assumes the hidden pocket holds one extra note beyond the 10. That risks overstating cash capacity, which is the very thing driving 44% of returns. It is flagged, but it shouldn't be in the copy. The line under the button also misses the chance to mention break-in.
to10: Treat 10 notes as the total. Use Tom's own 'brick' language. Add a way to measure whether the page cut returns. Put the break-in note or the warranty under the button.

strength: It states cash capacity conservatively: 10 notes in total, hidden pocket included. It adds a sound measurement plan with the correct numbers (3.3 and 1.0 per 100 orders) and a conversion guardrail. It also routes heavy-cash buyers to other wallets instead of losing them.
mistake: The break-in note isn't in the above-the-fold bullets or under the button, where it would catch the early 'too tight' returns best. The '10 to 11 mm' figure for 6 to 7 cards is interpolated, not in the data.
to10: Add 'snug for the first week, then it settles' to a bullet or under the button. Drop the interpolated 11 mm figure.

strength: It ties every email to my data and the numbers check out. It reports ₹48 vs ₹9 sales per click, matches each quiz answer to one product from Email 1, gives priced two-step routines with correct code maths (₹628.20, ₹898.20, ₹359.10), and adds a holdout with a ₹32,900-per-point projection.
mistake: Email 3 gives the sunscreen almost no 'what's inside' beyond SPF 50. Email 4 teaches all three actives at once, which edges toward the multi-active email I wanted to avoid. Email 5's CTA goes to the general collection instead of the matched routine.
to10: Name the sunscreen's filters and strength in Email 3. Point the Email 5 CTA at the matched two-product bundle. Tighten Email 4 so it reads as one idea.

strength: The Email 2 versions are well written for each quiz path, especially the sensitive-skin 'don't start with an acid' version. The calm sunscreen FAQ, the first-name greeting and the marketplace-buyer line are thoughtful touches.
mistake: Email 5 pushes all three products at ₹1,297 to everyone, including the sensitive and dry 19%. It also has the acid wash twice daily from day one, which contradicts the slow-start advice and my 'starter routine of 2–3, not the whole range' goal. Email 1 is a generic labeling welcome with no personalisation.
to10: Make Email 5 branch by quiz answer into a two-product routine. Personalise Email 1. Move the sunscreen email earlier. Add send times, a holdout test and a value estimate.

strength: It puts the 46 to 90 day 'slipping' group first with no discount and runs separate Monsoon Dark and ex-subscriber tracks. The group counts reconcile: 8,060, 11,640 and 10,700 all check out once ex-subscribers and Monsoon Dark buyers are taken out. The profit is worked per group net of the discount (₹557, ₹442, ₹385), with a gated subscription restart and a creative Monsoon Dark pre-order idea.
