mistake: There is no explicit break-even lift per group, only 'keep if gain is above zero'. The ex-subscriber message says 'we listened' but gives no proof that on-time delivery has recovered. Value covers first orders only and uses email reach only, which makes it conservative and leaves WhatsApp-only reach unvalued.
to10: Add the minimum lift each group needs to break even and put the actual on-time rate in the ex-subscriber email. Name the farm or estate in every draft. Show a 12-month view alongside the first-order view.

strength: The ex-subscriber track is very good: each cancel reason gets its own fix, the email shows proof of the recovered on-time rate, and the gate is clear. It also includes offer split tests (10% off vs free shipping), a minimum detectable lift, and an upside/downside range on the value.
mistake: It ranks the 91 to 180 day group first and leaves the cheapest 9,000 at-risk customers (46 to 90 days) to an always-on side nudge. It says ex-subscribers are pulled out of the other groups, but group A (13,100) never subtracts them. The 12-month value rests on an assumed 2 orders per returner, and reachable counts are not reduced for the holdout.
to10: Make the 46 to 90 day group wave one, with its own message and value line. Reconcile the group counts with the ex-subscriber carve-out. Size the value on reachable counts after the holdout and justify the repeat-order assumption.

strength: A clean, readable diagnosis. The proved-versus-to-check table has owners and dates. The $94 payback rule follows correctly from $71 first-order contribution plus a 31% repeat rate. Meta at $121 is correctly flagged as unrecoverable.
mistake: Gross profit impact is mostly given as High or Medium labels rather than sized numbers. The contribution baseline on the scorecard is 'set in week 1', and the flow target is 'pre-January level'. That leaves the board's main metric without a target.
to10: Size each move in points of contribution margin and compute today's contribution-after-ads baseline. Give a hard number for the flow-revenue target and a first-week action for each move.

strength: It derives contribution after ads, 13.6% then and 7.8% now, from the data, and the derivation checks out. Every move is sized in margin points with low, likely and high ranges and week-4 and week-8 kill lines. It also avoids double-counting move 4 with move 1. This is exactly what the board will ask for.
mistake: Some content is invented: the specific dates, the Black Friday timing and the 'practitioner yardstick' that flows should be about half of email revenue. The new-customer target of 'down 11% or better' is weak. The dense math makes it harder to read than it should be.
to10: Drop or flag the invented dates and benchmark, and set a real improvement target for new-customer orders. Move the working into an appendix so the plan reads at grade 8.

strength: It builds COD refusals into the money: it costs small-order refusals at about ₹1.04 lakh a month, explains why ₹499 sits on the refusal line, and adds a ₹49 COD fee under ₹499 as a third test. The bundle profits (₹537, ₹376, ₹359) and break-evens check out.
mistake: The baseline behind 'each adds about ₹262' is never explained. The ₹849 alternative's break-even of 487 orders doesn't match the per-order logic used elsewhere. Dense lakh figures and jargon like 'delivered gross profit per session' make it harder to read than it should be.
to10: Show how the ₹262 and ₹849 break-even figures are worked out. Give a separate COD vs prepaid free-shipping line as an option. Write the bundle names and copy in a warmer, more Plum voice.

strength: The serum price ladder (₹599 / ₹749 / ₹999) is clear and easy to read. The bundle profit maths is correct, and the reason for not doing an ₹849 duo (it would need about 700 step-ups a month) is sound.
mistake: The ₹599 recommendation depends on an unexplained guess that only 6% of orders sit between ₹499 and ₹598. If the 27% band is spread evenly, it is nearer 13%, which makes the ₹28k a month gain unreliable. It also barely uses RTO in the threshold decision, offers no COD-specific lever, and puts serum plus lip balm in two of its three bundles while skipping the body category.
to10: Size the ₹499–598 slice from the band data. Run the threshold maths on COD refusals as well as shipping fees. Swap the overlapping serum + lip balm bundle for a body or hair routine, and make lip balm a cart add-on.

strength: It leads with the in-app checkout fix and prices it correctly at about 558 orders and ₹34 lakh a month. Every run time and smallest effect is worked out from real session counts, and they check out (9.9%, 6.3%, 5.5%).
mistake: It has no test aimed at the firmness question. Firmness is only touched through review filter tabs. The calendar dates and the two-lane overlap add complexity I did not ask for.
to10: Add a plain-words firmness test. Show the funnel-by-browser maths in one simple table. Drop the invented calendar dates or tie them to real launch constraints.

strength: The diagnostic table splits the funnel by device and browser, and every rate in it is right. It ties the 4,130 in-app errors to the 4,800 lost carts. It adds an A/A test and event tracking before testing starts, and it covers firmness, which is the second-biggest chat topic.
mistake: Test 5 bundles the new hero image with the moved reviews. If it wins, I won't know which change worked.
to10: Split test 5 into two tests or justify the bundle. Give the profit value of each test's smallest effect, not only the one general 10% example.

strength: Every number checks out. That covers the RTO split by tier, ₹45k per RTO point, 63 RTOs per 1% prepaid shift and cart sizing. It also has a practical idea: move one agent to a 2 pm to midnight shift for the evening wave.
mistake: The prepaid nudge (pay_online_option_v1) is filed as Utility. It is a sales push, and Meta will likely recategorise it or flag quality. It also offers no prepaid incentive, so Tier 3 gets only a hold, not a stronger nudge.
to10: File the prepaid nudge as Marketing with a tiered incentive. Show RTO money and expected loss per order by tier. Add a net-saving metric. Skip confirmation for proven repeat COD buyers.

strength: The tiered economics are clear and they drive the actions: ₹70, ₹41 and ₹27 expected loss per COD order sets the ₹40 and ₹20 prepaid offers, and Tier 3 gets calls plus auto-cancel. Templates are categorised correctly, holdouts are built in, and there is a net-saving metric.
mistake: There is no staffing answer for the 31% evening chats beyond a bot menu, so size and exchange questions still wait until 10 am. The auto-cancel of silent Tier 3 orders may lose real sales, though the holdout partly covers this.
to10: Add an evening agent shift or bot answers for size and exchange. Add an after-hours response-time metric. Give a cart recovery sizing number like Output 1's.

strength: It catches the three big money issues: relaunch the paused Dad’s razor winner, cut the COD-heavy Starter Kit, and split Women 25-34 instead of killing the whole women’s razor line.
mistake: The 86% attribution assumption for prospecting is a bit made-up; I would want the team to use the Shopify/UTM haircut more consistently or label this as a sensitivity case, not the main truth.
to10: Use one clean attribution method, tighten the retargeting wording so 'cut' versus 'trim' is not confusing, and simplify the profit forecast so the team can act without debating assumptions.

strength: Very clear, practical, and it identifies the main actions: cut Starter Kit and Gift Sets, bring back Dad’s razor, isolate Women 25-34, and use daily rules instead of more reporting.
mistake: It says to scale ASC and Catalog even though the account is not clearly safe on Shopify-adjusted numbers; the scale gates are looser than its own 'safe line'.
to10: Make the budget more disciplined against the Shopify-adjusted break-even, hold more money in reserve until ASC proves the revived creative works, and judge retargeting/DPA more harshly for incrementality.

strength: It is built directly from our data: on-feet workers first, problem hooks first, mission as the close, and a $38 new-customer target tied to 90-day contribution.
mistake: The day-20 release rules mix TikTok-reported CPA, store tags, and survey reads in a slightly fuzzy way, and the holdout idea may be noisy for only 30 days.
to10: Tighten the measurement rules so the team knows exactly which source wins when reads disagree, and add the exact creator brief/output owners for the next 6 to 10 worker creators.

strength: It gets the main strategic call right: lead with real worker comfort, use the nurse and server Spark Ads, avoid discount and mission-first hooks, and judge against a $38 target.
mistake: It is a little more generic and less disciplined operationally: scaling/Smart+ starts early, the day-30 scorecard leans more on TikTok-claimed orders than I would like, and some rules are not as tightly tied to the economics.
to10: Make the budget phasing and scale rules more conservative until tracking is proven, remove Smart+ from month one, and make the final decision rule primarily Shopify new customers plus survey/lift against the $38 90-day break-even.

strength: It reads the data like an owner would: women are underfunded, quiet wheels are unused, work flyers need the belt-skip message, and scratch objections are handled instead of ignored.
mistake: A couple of concepts are still fairly conventional, especially the gift/static ideas, and the table plus detailed execution notes make it slightly heavier than needed.
to10: Tighten the layout a little, make the weaker concepts as fresh as the top three, and add one more creator/UGC-led execution to broaden the range.

strength: It finds the right big opportunities: work flyers skipping the belt, women lifting the bag alone, and quiet wheels as the underused hook.
mistake: It is a little looser on claims and execution details: the cabin sizer/dimensions point is not supported by the brief, and lines like 'No rattle' push beyond the approved spec/review language.
to10: Keep every claim inside the approved wording, make the test plan more statistically sensible, and sharpen the primary text so it feels more Mokobara and less generic ad copy.

strength: It uses the strongest signals correctly: 3 pm soda, blind taste test, taste before claims, and price handled plainly without a fake discount.
mistake: The family script has a small label-read beat that feels a bit stiff, and not every script uses all three approved claims if that was intended.
to10: Tighten the spoken lines even more for natural creator delivery, add first-frame ad disclosure inside each script, and make the price objection feel a little more emotional and less explanatory.

strength: It thinks like a performance producer: taste-led scripts, clear disclosure, hook testing, delivery specs, and a smart read that label-read ads got too much spend for their results.
mistake: The voice is a bit more media-buyer than Olipop; lines like 'Olipop paid me for this' and 'It's linked right there' feel less warm and less nostalgic.
to10: Make the creator lines feel more playful and less compliance-heavy, fix the inconsistency where the rules require all three approved claims but some scripts do not include them, and soften the disclosure language while keeping it compliant.

strength: It reads the data the way I would: bring back the paused winner, add the missing taste hook, and address ₹90 honestly.
mistake: It adds a fairly detailed media plan and budget assumption I did not ask for, and it may push the 1,000-word limit.
to10: Trim the run instructions, keep the launch plan, and double-check all character counts before trafficking.

strength: Very clean, usable, and correctly spots that the front-of-pack ad was tired, not dead, while making taste the big new test.
mistake: The six angles are a bit less varied; P1 and P5 are both transparency angles, and the copy is slightly more functional than sharp.
to10: Make the six primary texts more distinct, add a stronger 4 pm office-snack line, and sharpen the wit in the ad copy.

strength: It tackles the real return drivers head-on: cash capacity is stated early and often, card break-in is explained, and the copy uses exact carrying numbers without sounding defensive.
mistake: It adds an unasked-for measurement plan and fallback section, which makes the deliverable less clean as finished product page copy. The add-to-cart line also misses the chance to mention the first-week snugness.
to10: Trim the extra testing section from the page copy, move the break-in expectation into the add-to-cart line or above-fold bullets, and avoid lightly inferred numbers like 10 to 11 mm unless we have them.

strength: It puts the key buyer worries in the right places: cash, cards, front-pocket fit and the first-week tightness are all answered clearly and calmly.
mistake: It risks overstating capacity by saying the hidden pocket takes one more flat note, and it incorrectly implies all 5 to 12 cards are held in quick-access slots. The SEO title is also too long.
to10: Keep the cash promise to about 10 notes total, fix the quick-access wording, shorten the SEO title, and make the add-to-cart line work harder on the break-in or cash expectation issue.

strength: It uses the actual data well: leads with dark spots and niacinamide, fixes the sunscreen click-to-order leak by answering white cast and stickiness, and keeps beginners on a slow-start path.
mistake: The WhatsApp says 'Use it every other night for 2 weeks' for the matched product, which is wrong if the matched product is sunscreen and not ideal for every path.
to10: Fix the WhatsApp conditional copy by product, tighten the dry/sensitive path, and remove or adjust any deadline language if the code is not truly expiring.

strength: It is clear, structured, mostly on-brand, and correctly identifies the sunscreen problem, the dark-spot majority, and the beginner fear of irritation.
mistake: Email 5 pushes the same 3-product routine to everyone, including salicylic acid face wash morning and night, which goes against the brief's 'one idea' and beginner-safe approach.
to10: Make the final email segmented or choice-based instead of one full routine for all, keep the dark-spot path centred on niacinamide plus sunscreen, and avoid language like 'clear out oil' or anything that sounds too close to treatment claims.

strength: It reads the data like an operator: 46-90 day buyers first, Monsoon Dark as its own problem, and subscription win-back gated behind delivery fixes.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark draft does not actually name the closest replacement roast or farm, so the strongest segment still needs a better first message.
to10: Name the exact Monsoon Dark replacement, remove the arbitrary calendar dates, use combined email/WhatsApp reachable counts where possible, and tighten the message drafts to always name a farm or roast.

strength: The copy is strong, brand-safe, and the subscription section correctly leads with the delivery fix instead of a discount.
mistake: It largely misses the 46-90 day at-risk group as a main target, even though they are the cheapest win-back and directly tied to the repeat-rate fall.
to10: Put the existing 46-90 day customers first with counts, offers and value; separate them from the day-28 prevention flow; and recalc the forecast including that group and the 15% discount cases.

strength: It gets the real diagnosis right: Meta is the cost problem, linen is a return/product problem, and email capture/flows are switched half off. It also gives owners, stop rules, targets and a usable weekly scorecard.
mistake: Some projected contribution targets and gain estimates are a bit over-engineered and rest on assumptions that would need checking, especially the 18-month payback math and exact contribution lift by move.
to10: Tighten the assumptions, make the gain estimates slightly less precise where the data does not support precision, and explicitly show the return-rate movement from about 5.2% to 7.0%.
