mistake: It adds extra planning material beyond the ask and Script 3 leans on kids on camera, which can be more work and riskier to execute than a simpler family-angle version.
to10: Tighten a few lines, make every approved claim usage perfectly exact, and simplify the family script so it is easier to produce while keeping the same insight.

strength: It is clean, easy to follow, and sounds close to the brand voice while giving three usable creator scripts with strong hooks.
mistake: It slips on factual and compliance details: not all approved claims are handled carefully or fully, and the disclosure guidance is weaker and less embedded in the scripts than I would want for paid creator ads.
to10: Use the exact approved claims more consistently, address price and the winning data signals more sharply, and build in clearer paid partnership instructions inside each creator brief.

strength: It reads the data like an owner would: it brings back the paused transparency winner, spots taste as the missing hook, and addresses the ₹90 objection directly with launch-ready copy and a sensible first-4 test plan.
mistake: It invents a tighter 27-character headline/description limit than the owner's own note and uses review-stat phrasing like '1 in 4' that may be more than needed for simple ad copy.
to10: Use the owner's stated display guidance more cleanly, keep the launch plan, and tighten any lines that feel slightly over-explained or legally debatable around review quoting.

strength: It also sees the key opportunities: revive front-of-pack, test taste, and tackle price honestly, with a good spread of distinct angles.
mistake: It adds made-up operating assumptions the brief did not give, including budget, test structure, and a live-control setup, and one primary text says 'our protein bar' without the approved 12 g claim while another headline-description pairing risks sounding less on-brand than the stronger copy in o1.
to10: Strip out the invented media plan details, stay tightly inside the approved claims and brief, and focus the answer on cleaner launch-ready copy plus a simpler first-4 test recommendation.

strength: It directly addresses the two biggest return drivers with clear, honest numbers above the fold and a calm Bellroy-like trade-off framing.
mistake: It adds an unverified claim that the hidden pocket can take an extra flat note, which risks overstating capacity on the exact issue causing returns.
to10: Remove the extra-note assumption, put the break-in note under the add-to-cart button, and keep every capacity statement absolutely consistent.

strength: It is tightly aligned to the business problem: it leads with real carry numbers, sets cash expectations honestly, explains break-in well, and even proposes how to measure whether the page reduces returns without hurting sales.
mistake: It wanders outside the requested deliverable with the measurement section, and the line under add-to-cart misses the chance to use the more important first-week snugness message.
to10: Swap the measurement section for tighter product-page copy, move the snug-for-the-first-week expectation to the add-to-cart area, and make the voice a touch more polished and distinctive to Bellroy.

strength: It reads the business well: it leads with dark spots, tackles beginner fear, and gives sunscreen its own email that answers white cast and stickiness directly.
mistake: Email 5 pushes a three-product routine too broadly, which is a bit much for a brand whose buyers want fewer steps and for an audience that is mostly new to actives.
to10: Keep the same structure but make the final email more clearly branched by skin concern, and tighten a few risky lines like specific sunscreen application claims unless verified on-page.

strength: It turns the data into a sharper plan: quiz-based matching from email 1, a clear beginner path, a focused sunscreen objection email, and stronger operational detail on exits, cart pause, and measurement.
mistake: A few additions drift beyond the brief or certainty of the data, like evening-send justification and some extra testing/projection detail that an owner may not need in the finished asset.
to10: Trim the non-essential optimisation notes, keep only the deliverable, and slightly simplify a few lines so the final output feels even more publish-ready with less implementation clutter.

strength: It spots the real causes of lapse and builds the programme around them: Monsoon Dark gets its own track, ex-subscribers are gated on fixing delivery, and 46 to 90 days is treated as prevention rather than true win-back.
mistake: It says group A is 91 to 180 days but then calls it the biggest group and excludes Monsoon Dark in a way that does not quite add up, so the segment math and naming need a quick clean-up before use.
to10: Tighten the segment definitions and reachable counts, explicitly include the 46 to 90 day at-risk flow in the ranked table, and make the profit model a little more conservative and easier to audit.

strength: It prioritises well, especially by putting the 46 to 90 day group first and holding ex-subscribers until the delivery problem is fixed, and it gives a sensible holdout-based measurement plan.
mistake: Several numbers and assumptions are shaky or wrong enough to weaken trust: the dated launch plan is oddly specific, the 68-day lapse rule is invented from the median, reachable counts rely only on email despite WhatsApp being available, and the ex-subscriber profit math looks inconsistent.
to10: Clean up the maths and assumptions, remove arbitrary dates and unsupported rules, and make the Monsoon Dark recommendation more direct and ready to send instead of adding speculative ideas like a pre-order lot.

strength: It cleanly separates what the data proves from what still needs checking, then turns that into a practical 90-day plan with ranked moves, owners, stop rules and a useful weekly scorecard.
mistake: It is a little conservative on new ideas beyond fixing the obvious leaks, so it gives me fewer upside bets once the core issues are stabilised.
to10: Add one well-bounded growth test beyond the core fixes, such as a swatch or product-discovery offer, with clear success and stop criteria.

strength: It brings more modelling and a wider range of ideas, including explicit scenario sizing and one bolder test, which helps me see possible upside.
mistake: It overreaches on a few assumptions and calculations that are not solid enough to steer the business, and some recommendations are too specific or off-brand for what the brief actually proved.
to10: Tighten the maths to only what the data supports, simplify the plan, and remove or soften the more speculative claims and tactics so I can trust it without checking every line.

strength: It answers the full brief with three sensible bundles, real threshold math, COD/RTO logic, and a safe test plan tied to delivered profit.
mistake: It makes a few assumptions and projections that feel more confident than the data supports, and the lead bundle choice adds lip balm where the clearest customer-built bundle is face wash plus serum.
to10: Tighten the math behind the monthly projections, make the face wash + serum duo the clear hero bundle, and simplify a few dense sections so the key recommendation is easier to act on fast.

strength: It is easy to read and does a good job protecting the serum reorder by avoiding a ₹699 threshold.
mistake: The ₹599 free-shipping recommendation rests on a made-up slice of orders between ₹499 and ₹598, and it leaves out the strongest existing bundle signal by not making face wash + serum the main hero bundle.
to10: Use only defensible numbers from the data, center the proven face wash + serum routine, and work COD/RTO into the threshold recommendation more rigorously.

strength: It spots the in-app checkout issue as the first priority, sizes the upside in money, and gives a ranked plan with practical test mechanics tied to the evidence in the brief.
mistake: A few testing choices feel shakier than they should, especially overlapping tests and some sample-size/runtime claims that are presented with more certainty than the data really supports.
to10: Tighten the experimental design and sample-size logic, simplify the schedule, and make the copy/examples a little more consistent with a mobile-first Wakefit page.

strength: It is very easy to read, correctly calls out the in-app checkout bug, and keeps the plan anchored in real customer questions like delivery date, size, firmness and EMI.
mistake: It misses some of the strongest asks from the brief by underplaying the need to quantify test sensitivity honestly and by bundling changes or adding assumptions that are less grounded in the page data.
to10: Separate cleaner tests, show more rigorous run-time and detectable-effect logic, and sharpen the prioritisation so the owner can act with more confidence.

strength: It understands the business problem well, especially the tiered COD risk and the need to add shipped and out-for-delivery updates to cut order-status chats.
mistake: The after-hours menu is thinner than it should be, and the owner specifically wanted short reply scripts for 5 questions while the automated menu only covers some of them.
to10: Add a fuller after-hours button flow, tighten a couple of template/category choices, and make the pincode-based operational rules even more explicit for agents and automation.

strength: It brings strong commercial thinking, especially holdouts, net-savings logic, and the bold Tier 3 treatment including testing a partial advance.
mistake: It mixes marketing into places that should stay utility-safe, invents discounting without any brief support, and includes a likely invalid template/button setup that makes it less ready to submit.
to10: Keep the strong testing mindset but remove unsupported discounts, make the WhatsApp template design policy-safe and operationally realistic, and simplify it into a cleaner owner-ready submission pack.

strength: It finds the three big money signals: relaunch the paused creator winner, cut the Starter Kit COD trap, and split Women Body Razor to 25-34 instead of killing it.
mistake: The daily rule to pause new ads after only ₹800 with no purchase is a bit too tight for this account and could kill ads before they get a fair read.
to10: Tighten the action thresholds slightly, make the Shopify-adjusted view the main scorecard throughout, and add the Starter Kit comeback condition as prepaid/confirmed-COD or blocked high-RTO pincodes.

strength: It also catches the main account truths: the paused Dad’s razor ad matters, Starter Kit is a COD/RTO problem, and Women 25-34 is the good pocket.
mistake: It says no ad set earns a raise but then raises the unproven UGC test materially, invents dates, and uses a made-up 86% attribution assumption for prospecting without enough support.
to10: Remove the invented date and attribution haircut, fix the contradictory calls, reduce the UGC budget, and put more conditional money behind ASC once the winning creator ad is back.

strength: It uses our actual signals well: worker feet first, problem-first hooks, Spark Ads from the nurse and server, the $38 90-day payback line, and a Monday-ready setup list.
mistake: The day-30 incrementality check is useful but a little soft; I would want the survey and Shopify/new-customer read to be more central than TikTok-claimed orders.
to10: Tighten the measurement plan with a clearer Shopify/survey/lift decision rule, and spell out creator rights/briefing dates so we are not dependent on the March-licensed posts.

strength: The measurement thinking is strong: it does not trust TikTok ROAS alone, uses store tags, survey, lift, and even suggests a holdout.
mistake: It feels a bit more like a media buyer memo than a Bombas team plan; the creative and brand handling are good but not quite as warm or as operationally complete as Output 1.
to10: Add the comment/brand-safety plan, make the creative calendar more Monday-ready, soften a few media-buyer phrases, and avoid anything that could make donation feel like the lead.

strength: It reads the data like an owner would: quiet wheels, women travellers, cabin-only work flyers, and scratch concerns all show up in the right places.
mistake: The price-reframe concept feels a little more value-led than Mokobara’s usual understated design voice, and one or two lines are slightly too absolute around skipping the belt.
to10: Tighten the brand voice on the price concept, remove any absolute-sounding travel promises, and turn the top three into final shoot scripts with shot timings and captions.

strength: The copy is clean, calm and close to the Mokobara voice. The top three choices are exactly the right lanes: belt-skip, lift-it-yourself, and quiet wheels.
mistake: A few execution details need tightening for claim safety, especially the cabin sizer/dimensions idea and phrases like “no rattle” or “just glide” when not clearly framed as buyer language.
to10: Keep the voice, but make every claim sit inside the approved specs, add clearer headlines and final ad copy for each concept, and give a stronger testing plan than the very low spend threshold.

strength: It really uses the data: taste first, 3 pm habit, price objection, variety pack details, and paid disclosure are all built into the scripts.
mistake: It is a bit overbuilt and likely over the word limit, with extra testing and rights sections I did not ask for; a few creator lines sound more like a marketer than a real person.
to10: Trim the extra strategy sections, polish the spoken lines to feel more natural, and keep only the most shoot-ready guidance while preserving the strong disclosure and price handling.

strength: The scripts are clean, easy to shoot, and sound warm and natural for creators without drifting into banned health language.
mistake: The paid-ad disclosure is weaker inside the actual scripts, and the price objection is mostly handled in only one script instead of being answered more consistently.
to10: Add clear on-screen or spoken ad disclosure in each script, handle the $3-per-can objection more directly, and make the family script a little more careful with kids and claims.

strength: It gets the big calls right: revive the paused winner, lead with taste, and address the ₹90 objection honestly, all in a voice that feels close to The Whole Truth.
mistake: It adds quite a bit of media-plan detail and assumed budget that was not asked for, and it may run a little long for the brief.
to10: Trim the extra testing mechanics, keep the launch plan tighter, and double-check every character count against actual Meta placements.

strength: It is clean, practical, and correctly reads the data: the front-of-pack ad was tired, taste is the missing hook, and price needs to be tested upfront.
mistake: The six angles are not quite different enough: transparency appears twice, taste and texture overlap, and the office-snack/protein angles are less fully covered.
to10: Make the six copy routes more distinct: transparency, taste, no added sugar, protein, 4 pm snack, and price/value, with a little more blunt wit in the lines.

strength: It leads with the exact carrying numbers, handles the cash and break-in trade-offs honestly, and speaks directly to Tom and Jen’s doubts without hype.
mistake: The add-to-cart support line misses the chance to mention the first-week snugness, and the extra measurement section is useful but not product-page copy.
to10: Move the break-in expectation closer to purchase, possibly under the add-to-cart button, and trim the non-page testing notes before publishing.

strength: It is clear, practical and honest, with strong above-the-fold handling of cards, cash, thickness, break-in and the small coin pouch.
mistake: It risks overstating cash capacity by saying the hidden pocket takes one more flat note on top of the 10-note section, which could worsen the exact return reason we are trying to reduce.
to10: Keep the cash promise conservative and consistent, shorten the SEO title, and soften or remove the more internal-sounding review-count and returns language.

strength: It is very close to a usable flow: clear timing, exit rule, full email copy, calm voice, strong beginner guidance, and a dedicated sunscreen email that answers white cast and stickiness.
mistake: Email 5 turns into a one-size-fits-all 3-step routine and pushes Salicylic Acid 2% face wash to everyone, including dark spot, dry, and sensitive users. That goes against the simple matched-start approach and may worry beginners.
to10: Keep the final reminder personalised by concern, make sunscreen plus niacinamide the main dark-spot path, avoid recommending salicylic acid unless the quiz says oiliness/acne, and tighten a few claims and price roundings before loading into Klaviyo.

strength: It uses the data like an owner would: leads with quiz-based product matching, fixes the sunscreen leak, handles beginner fear, adds cart pauses and holdouts, and even sizes the revenue impact of lifts.
mistake: Some copy is a little more operational than customer-facing, and Email 2 calls it an active plan even for the sunscreen path. It needs a final polish pass for warmth and exact wording.
to10: Make the customer-facing emails feel slightly less like blocks from a strategy doc, adjust the sunscreen/non-active wording, and turn the conditional sections into final Klaviyo-ready variants.

strength: It spots the two big business truths: Monsoon Dark needs its own track, and subscription win-back must wait until delivery is fixed. It also correctly starts with the 46 to 90 day at-risk group and uses holdouts to measure true lift.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark message asks people to take a quiz instead of naming a clear closest replacement coffee, which is the main fix this group needs.
to10: Name the exact replacement roast or farm for Monsoon Dark, tidy a few over-specific dates and assumptions, and make the first drafts a little warmer and less operational.

strength: The writing sounds very close to the brand: warm, simple, not discount-led, and clear about fixing the real reason people left.
mistake: It does not put the 46 to 90 day customers first as a win-back group, even though they are the cheapest and most urgent people to bring back.
to10: Move the 46 to 90 day group to the top of the programme, subtract holdouts from the value table, and make the financial model a little more conservative and first-order focused.

strength: It finds the real three leaks quickly: Meta, switched-off lifecycle revenue, and linen returns, then turns them into ranked actions with owners, thresholds, and a weekly operating scorecard.
mistake: It is a little over-precise in places, with assumptions presented almost like facts, and the dated Black Friday reference could be wrong or distracting.
to10: Tighten the language, remove the calendar-specific references, make the linen fix feel a bit more urgent in the ranking, and label the more speculative contribution math more clearly.

strength: It is clean, owner-friendly, and very easy to act on. The diagnosis is right and the tone fits the brand better than a hard discount-led growth plan.
mistake: It overcorrects on linen by saying to stop promoting it anywhere, not just pull it from Meta prospecting until the shrink issue is understood, which could unnecessarily hurt revenue.
to10: Add more quantified impact by move, sharper weekly thresholds, first-week steps for every owner, and a clearer split between cutting bad Meta spend and rebuilding Meta once linen and tracking are fixed.

strength: It uses the real buying signals: face wash + serum, lip balm as the add-on, and COD/RTO leakage under ₹500. The bundle economics and safe test plan are strong enough to act on.
mistake: The lead glow bundle may be a little too built-up at ₹999 instead of first testing the simpler face wash + serum routine, and some projections rely on assumptions that should be checked in the order export.
to10: Add a simpler face wash + serum bundle or test it against the ₹999 trio, tighten the assumptions behind the threshold ranges, and polish the customer-facing copy slightly more in Plum’s cheerful voice.

strength: It is clear, customer-aware, and protects the vitamin C serum reorder by avoiding a jump to ₹699. The bundle ladder on the serum page is a good merchandising idea.
mistake: The ₹599 threshold math is weak: it underestimates the affected order band and does not use the COD/RTO issue deeply enough. It also turns lip balm into a discounted main bundle rather than mainly using it as the natural cart add-on.
to10: Rework the shipping threshold with the actual order bands and RTO costs, treat lip balm primarily as an add-on to cross the line, and include a stronger second-category routine such as body or hair with clearer break-even logic.

strength: It catches the in-app checkout bug as a ship-now fix, sizes the money well, and then ranks tests around the real customer doubts: delivery, size, firmness, EMI, and trust.
mistake: The test plan needs a cleaner experiment design after the checkout fix. Some sizing is based on the old baseline, and the two-at-once schedule could create interaction issues unless set up as a proper factorial test.
to10: Refresh the baselines after the in-app fix, tighten the sample-size/MDE maths for each metric, and make the parallel-test setup safer and easier for the team to run.

strength: It gives the right first call: fix the broken in-app checkout before testing, with a clear profit range. It also has smart reasoning, especially that delivery-date visibility may reduce add-to-cart but still lift orders.
mistake: Some detectable-effect numbers for the two-week add-to-cart tests look too optimistic, and it misses a plain firmness test even though firmness is the second-biggest chat topic.
to10: Correct the MDE maths, avoid invented calendar dates unless confirmed, and replace either the hero-image or reviews test with a stronger firmness-and-trial clarity test.

strength: It uses the data like an owner would: Tier 3 gets special treatment, order-status WhatsApps reduce chat load, and the templates mostly respect Utility vs Marketing rules.
mistake: The prepaid discount and Tier 3 cancel rule need careful testing before full rollout, because they could either give away margin or cancel some orders that would have delivered.
to10: Tighten the final template copy a little more into Snitch voice, confirm exact courier/Meta rules with the provider, and make the discount or ₹99 advance a controlled test rather than a default.

strength: It is clear, practical, and covers the main flows, scripts, after-hours automation, and weekly numbers in a usable structure.
mistake: It puts the prepaid switch nudge in Utility, assumes a 7-day exchange policy, and does not target Tier 3 risk strongly enough even though that is where half the RTO cost sits.
to10: Reclassify the prepaid nudge as Marketing, remove unverified exchange-policy claims, add a stronger Tier 3 COD confirmation/prepaid/hold flow, and make delivery-day messages include tracking and reattempt handling consistently.

strength: Finds the three rupee stories the owner cares about most — the paused ₹250 creator video, the COD trap Starter Kit at ₹463 vs ₹271, and the women 25–34 split at ₹414 — and turns each into a concrete Monday move with a budget that adds up to ₹5,60,000.
mistake: The dual safe/break-even line system is clever but slightly self-contradicting: it labels Beard Kit as profitable at ₹429 vs safe ₹333 while the ₹394 break-even line says the opposite, and the 'ASC lost ₹29,000 on Meta count' note is muddied by the ₹282 line. A few break-even figures (Women ₹435) are not shown in the workings, so the reader has to trust them.
to10: Show the per-ad-set break-even arithmetic in one line each (order value × COD mix), and simplify to one break-even line per ad set — the owner asked for decisions, not a two-tier system that occasionally sends mixed signals.

strength: The state-split retargeting experiment is a genuinely rare, testable idea that answers a real question ('does retargeting pay at all?') with a read date and a rupee bar of 39 orders — plus break-even is shown transparently per order type (prepaid ₹450, COD ₹325, blended ₹394).
mistake: Dated the plan '14 to 27 November' as if real, and the reserve-heavy structure (₹1,49,100 held back, ₹4,10,900 committed) makes it less of a budget split than output 1's; also it cuts retargeting outright (to ₹28,000) which contradicts the 'fix' spirit of the owner notes and risks losing warm buyers. Voice drifts drier — 'on Meta's count' repeated constantly is analyst-speak, not the confident straight-talk the brand wants.
to10: Align dates to 'the next 14 days,' keep the state split but run it while still spending on retargeting at a floor, and rewrite the calls in the brand's straight-talking voice so a founder could forward the table to the team without translation.

strength: Ties every rule to our own numbers (the $27.10 first-order and $38 90-day break-even, the nurse/server watch times, the Meta hook costs) and gives dated owners, dollar kill/scale lines and a day-30 decision table I could hand over Monday.
mistake: The day-21 to 30 release rule leans on TikTok-reported and store-tagged reads with a $50 store-tag threshold that is loose, and the multi-read 'two of three agree' logic is more machinery than a launch team will actually run cleanly; also leans on 'both creators' making new posts as if guaranteed.
to10: Tighten the day-30 scoring to one primary read (blended lift or survey) with the others as checks, tighten the store-tag threshold to something like $45, and confirm the two creators are contracted for the two new posts.

strength: Very readable, clean creative concept table with plain brand-safe wording rules and a sensible 'handle price inside the ad' instinct.
mistake: It splits budget into a separate SCALE campaign that opens day 8 and mixes Smart+ in while also claiming cleaner reads, uses a looser scale bar ($34) and a $45 hold band that don't match our $38 break-even, and sets a 790-first-order pass bar that ignores the learning period and the $27.10 first-order reality.
to10: Anchor every threshold to the $38 90-day break-even, drop Smart+ and the early second campaign for month one, and give a single day-30 decision rule with an explicit lift or survey read rather than four pass/fail rows.

strength: Ties every concept to a real signal in my data and tells me exactly what each one tests, with a first-three pick I believe in.
mistake: Some hooks put review-table quotes in the buyer's mouth as voiceover copy; I'd want those trimmed to clearly-attributed lines before launch.
to10: Storyboard frames or shot lists per concept, and a slightly tighter primary-text length per format.

strength: Sharp front-loaded framing of the two data stories and a strong, concrete test-spend plan with per-concept budgets.
mistake: The table-first structure and long primary texts read more like a media plan than brand creative, and the voice drifts to spec-listing; hooks lean on quoted reviews where I asked for my own lines.
to10: Full draft primary text and visual scripts in our voice, not just a hook and a scene note, plus lighter colour lead stated up front rather than buried in the rules.

strength: Uses the owner's own numbers and customer language to lead every angle (taste test, 3 pm swap, game-day cooler), names the price objection on camera, and adds a concrete test plan with cut thresholds.
mistake: A little over-packed and production-team-flavoured at moments (test plan, bolder move, strict hook cut-offs) for UGC, and the 'Ad' on first frame is rigid; also claim lines are crammed into mouthfuls that may trip a real creator.
to10: Tighten each script's spoken lines to natural, grade-6 breezy speech, trim the extra test-plan/metadata, and give creators one clearer sentence of freedom plus a softer, platform-correct disclosure instruction.

strength: Clean, shootable scripts with natural spoken lines, real customer hooks, explicit price handling and a strong creative-brief tone that creators can act on immediately.
mistake: Less analytical than the owner's data allowed; it doesn't use the cost-per-purchase insight or price comment share as explicitly, and its disclosure guidance is a bit generic (caption '#ad' and toggle) rather than fully platform-specific.
to10: Mine the comment and paid-ad data for the opening choices and test plan (taste test over label, $3 objection) and add sharper creator rules on disclosure, forbidden words and claim wording.

strength: Correctly reads the paused 'flip the pack' ad as fatigued not failed, revives it with fresh words, and leads the launch set with transparency and taste while naming the ₹90 price objection directly.
mistake: P3 texture and P4 sugar sit near the held-back tail, so the six angles skew slightly toward review-quote proof and the voice leans a touch more analyst than blunt-witty in the rationale sections.
to10: Punchier, more human primary texts in our own blunt voice rather than near-quoted review lines, plus a slightly wider spread across all six angles.

strength: Sharpest owner-level thinking: brings back the front-of-pack winner, names the price head-on, targets Aditya and Priya by name, and specifies a full test budget, control cell and read rules that an owner could run today.
mistake: Character claims sit right on the limits and the ₹84,000 budget is an assumed number stated with confidence, so a few lines may truncate or mislead if the real spend differs.
to10: Trim every line a few characters under the limits for safety and flag the budget as an assumption rather than a data-derived rate.

strength: Cash capacity stated as a number everywhere it matters (subtitle, bullet, spec, FAQ, button line), with the trade-off framed calmly and the break-in expectation set in three places.
mistake: The SEO title runs 48 characters but reads slightly padded with the pipe, and the 'How to tell it worked' / assumptions section is process detail that would need trimming for a live page; also assumes hidden pocket is included in the 10 notes without flagging it may be one more.
to10: Confirm whether the hidden pocket adds capacity and state it, tighten the meta and subtitle so the cash number sits without repetition, and add the outer dimensions if available for a truer front-pocket answer.

strength: 'What fits, in real life' scenarios and the plain 'what doesn't fit' line make the trade-offs vivid and human, with a distinctive closing paragraph that would suit Tom and Jen.
mistake: Invents an extra 'one more flat note' in the hidden pocket and a coin-pouch parking-meter line, and the SEO title (67 chars) and subtitle both push the primary money line below the fold; also gives 8-card thickness implicitly as 'still closes flat' where data only supports flat at 8.
to10: Drop the invented hidden-pocket capacity, bring the SEO title under 60 characters, state the 8-card thickness or avoid the claim, and keep the strong scenario section while tightening the cash number into the subtitle.

strength: Uses the data to make decisions: niacinamide as default pick, an entire email aimed at the white cast and stickiness doubts, per-quiz product branching, a cart-pause rule, and a WhatsApp placed 24 hours before the code expires.
mistake: The WhatsApp line says 'ends tomorrow' while the code was set to expire 14 days after sign-up; if the WhatsApp goes on day 13 that is technically fine, but the email/WhatsApp timing line ('day 13, 24 hours before the code ends') needs checking against the actual code expiry, since 14 days from sign-up would end on day 14, not after the WhatsApp.
to10: Tighten one factual seam (exact code expiry vs. WhatsApp day) and add one plain photo or swatch guidance for the sunscreen, which the owner flagged as the bolder move.

strength: Warm, calm, on-brand voice with a clear 3-step routine answer and a clean exit rule; Email 3 on starting slowly is the best-written fear-killer of the two.
mistake: Priorities are slightly off: the sunscreen email comes fourth after the starter email, and Email 5 pushes all three products as a ₹1,167 routine rather than leading with the one product that fits the quiz answer, which undercuts the 'one product, not ten' promise and oversells to a nervous beginner.
to10: Make Email 5 a per-quiz 'one product plus sunscreen' recommendation, and lead the series with the dark-spot path, since 44% name uneven tone.

strength: It ranks the at-risk 46-90 day group first, gives Monsoon Dark its own named track with a draft that names the blend, gates ex-subscribers behind a delivery fix, and includes a bold one-lot Monsoon Dark pre-order idea.
mistake: The projection table is dense and its return-rate assumptions (e.g. 6-12% for ex-subscribers) feel optimistic; the 'bolder move' and cold-brew timing add complexity that could dilute focus.
to10: A tighter one-page summary of the ranked plan and numbers, with the projection assumptions justified in a line each and the pre-order idea held as a clearly optional appendix.

strength: Reads cleanly and names the real reasons (delivery, discontinued blend), gives each cancel reason its own fix, and states the gross-profit per order and discount cost plainly.
mistake: Puts the 91-180 day group first and treats the 46-90 day drifters only as a side 'stop the leak' note, so the cheapest-to-win group is not the headline; lift assumptions are also loose.
to10: Lead with the 46-90 day at-risk group as wave 1, and tighten the lift and gross-profit math so each group's return assumption is defended, not just stated.

strength: It does the owner's own math for them: derives the 7.8% contribution baseline, prices each move in points of contribution margin with low/likely/high ranges, and ties every move to a week-4 and week-8 line so the scorecard is a real operating tool.
mistake: Voice drifts into analyst shorthand — 'w × (−11%) + (1 − w) × 6% = −4%', 'sizing:', '0.89 × $104 ÷ $78' — which is not how we'd talk to a customer or a team, and the six-move table plus dense formulas make it heavy to read first pass.
to10: Rewrite the working and sizing in plain sentences, drop one level of formula from the main text (keep it in an appendix), and add a half-line of our warm tone per move so it reads like us, not a consulting memo.

strength: Reads exactly like an owner would want to circulate: plain language, the stops stated crisply, the checks table assigned with owners and dates, and brand voice respected ('Touch it before you commit'), with the swatch idea woven in rather than bolted on.
mistake: Leaves the contribution baseline as 'set baseline in week 1' instead of computing it, and its payback math is looser — the $23k–$41k saving per $100k cut is a range without shown working, and the move table ranks by 'high/medium/low' rather than ranked gross-profit numbers, so ranking is softer than the brief asked.
to10: Do the contribution and payback math explicitly to the same rigor as its diagnosis, convert the impact column into ranked points of contribution margin with low/likely/high, and set a real day-90 target instead of deferring the baseline.

strength: Bundle ladder on the serum page (serum, serum+lip balm, full routine) with a per-bundle break-even the owner can check, and an honest 'why not ₹699' comparison.
mistake: The face wash + serum pair, the signature routine, only appears as a discounted twist in the ₹999 trio; the ₹749 serum+lip balm is a small step, not the routine Kavya asked for. Also the volume assumptions (17k orders/month) and the 'shipping costs ₹11.9 lakh' framing rest on invented slices.
to10: Make the top pair the flagship routine at a modest saving, show its margin at ₹849 and at ₹999 side by side, tie the threshold choice to COD refusal money explicitly, and label every modelled number as a test assumption.

strength: Sharpest insight in the job: keeping ₹499 because it sits on the COD refusal line, plus a clean lip balm cart lever with real money, and a ₹49 COD fee as a separate test.
mistake: The flagship Glow Routine at ₹999 gives up ₹35 on the 1,033 pair buyers who already buy face wash + serum; it sells the existing pair cheaper instead of a step up, and the three bundles all land at ₹749/₹999 without a clear low-price entry for Ishita.
to10: Lead with the face wash + serum routine as the hero at a small, profitable saving, use the lip balm as the threshold lever, and add a break-even table that shows what the discount costs on current pair buyers.

strength: The bug is called out first with the money, the browser split is read properly, and the tests are ranked by expected impact with honest sample maths in plain words.
mistake: The five-test schedule runs two tests at once on shared page real estate with interactio checks left late; and test 3 (firmness) is weaker and less evidenced than the firmer review-relocation idea, so one ranking slot may be soft.
to10: Tie each test tighter to one evidence line (34%, 19%, 17%, 14%, 81%) with a scannable table up front, and state the ship-rule and stop-early rules as explicitly as the lane plan.

strength: Precise arithmetic on the in-app gap (23.8% vs 53.3%, 1,860 checkouts, 558 orders, ₹17-34 lakh), calendar dates, and a clear two-lane schedule with a proper ship rule.
mistake: Add-to-cart as the main metric on three of five tests despite mobile converting at 0.56% and a fix that removes the reason to reach checkout; it ranks reviews above the bigger firmness doubt and the hero image as a test despite thinnest evidence.
to10: Use orders per session (or checkout reach where it fits) as the main metric wherever it pays, demote the hero image to a ship item, and write the trial and delivery lines in the brand's own words.

strength: Strong, warm creator scripts with three distinct, data-backed angles and a clean three-hook testing plan.
mistake: Paid disclosure is only a global rule/caption note, not written into each script’s first frame or spoken line, and production deliverables/rights are missing.
to10: Bake the Meta/TikTok paid partnership disclosure into each script and add creator deliverables and usage rights without losing the warm, natural voice.

strength: Most production-ready: every script has on-screen and spoken ad disclosure, exact claims, price math, deliverables/rights, and a budgeted hook test plan.
mistake: A few continuity/creator-naturalness slips, such as the blind-test ending on “both clink cans” after one drink was a regular soda in a glass.
to10: Fix the continuity issues and loosen a few lines so they sound more like a real creator and less like an ad read, while keeping the compliance and test plan.

strength: The branching in Email 2: three complete versions, each with its own subject line, one product and a slow-start instruction, mapped to the quiz shares (55/26/19). That is exactly the 'tell me which serum is for me' problem solved, and the voice across Emails 1-4 is calm, plain and unmistakably ours.
mistake: Email 5 throws away the whole safety argument: it gives everyone a morning-and-night routine built on Salicylic Acid 2% face wash (twice a day) and pushes a three-product bundle at beginners who were told one product at a time. It also contradicts the sensitivity branch that said 'don't start with an acid'.
to10: Keep the branch, then make Email 5 branch too: send each person only their own two-product morning/night routine, cap the acid at once a day, drop the bundle price push, and name the active and strength in at least two subject lines.

strength: It reads like a marketer who did the maths: ₹48 of sales per niacinamide click against ₹9 for sunscreen, 77% of sunscreen questions on white cast/stickiness/makeup, an entry filter so past buyers never get a first-order code, a cart pause, and a holdout test whose numbers I could verify (157 sign-ups a day, ~47 orders per point, ~₹32,900).
mistake: Craft slips exactly where a copywriter should not: no 'Hi {{ first_name }}' or sign-off in Emails 1-4, and the merge tag {{ person|lookup:'welcome_code' }} is not valid Klaviyo syntax, so the code would render blank in the one email that must deliver it.
to10: Add greetings and a signed-off human line to each email, fix the code merge tag, and swap the label-reading email (nice, but it burns a scarce slot in a 14-day window) for a social-proof reminder with the review line and the deadline.

strength: The clearest read of the business: it names the real problem (new-customer cost off Meta, linen returns, switched-off email capture) in plain language, uses the customer's own words, and is honest about its assumptions. I could send this Monday with light edits.
mistake: It says the moves are 'ranked by gross profit impact and effort' but only gives High/Medium/Low, so the ranking is softer than the brief asked for. It also lists 'Meta customers do not pay back within 18 months' under what's proved, when that leans on the blended 31% repeat rate applying to Meta buyers too.
to10: Put a real number on each move's gross-profit impact and effort (low/likely/high), add week-4 and week-8 gates, and add action thresholds to the scorecard so I know when to stop or double down.

strength: It builds a real contribution-margin baseline (13.6% to 7.8%) from the data and ranks moves by a quantified gain-divided-by-effort with low/likely/high ranges, week-4/8 gates, and per-line action thresholds. That is a model I can actually run, not just prose.
mistake: False precision and density. The 12.9% day-90 target stacks several optimistic projections on layered assumptions, the derivation is hard to scan, and there are small internal inconsistencies (contribution works out nearer 7.6% than 7.8%; the flow-revenue sizing looks slightly generous). It also invents a start date the brief never gave.
to10: Lead with a plain one-page summary and one 'likely' number per move, trim the model's precision to what the data supports, fix the rounding so every figure ties out, and keep the thresholds, which are the best part.

strength: Every ad set gets a rupee verdict and the three owner signals (revive the paused creator video, split out women 25-34, kill the COD-trap Starter Kit) are all caught and priced.
mistake: The two break-even lines (₹282 safe / ₹394 break-even) are a clever device but the per-ad-set safe numbers in the table aren't shown to be derived consistently, so a finance-minded reader has to trust them.
to10: Show the safe/break-even math per ad set in one column each (order value × COD mix × 72% haircut) so the table is auditable, and trim the creative section slightly to keep the budget and rules the spine.

strength: The reserve-release rules and the retargeting holdout test are genuinely owner-grade thinking, and the forecast lines (store-count vs Meta-count) frame the decision honestly.
mistake: It cuts retargeting (frequency 6.8 is a real signal but ₹289 cost vs ₹358 profit per order is the one ad set that clearly pays) and spreads the fix across too many conditional branches, so the one-page decision is harder to act on Monday morning.
to10: Simplify to one committed number per ad set with a single reserve rule, and keep the retargeting holdout as a clearly optional appendix rather than mixing it into the main call.

strength: Ties every rule to Bombas' numbers, leads with on-feet shift workers, and builds a phased plan with dollar kill/scale lines that a team can execute Monday morning.
mistake: The 90-day break-even calculation is opaque and may be off by a few dollars, but it doesn't change the $38 target.
to10: Clearer math on the 90-day break-even and a simple note on how the $57 stop line was chosen.

strength: Clear set-up checklist and a good mix of creative concepts, with detailed tracking and a structured Day-30 scorecard.
mistake: The budget phasing adds to $29,000, not $30,000, and the Day-30 benchmarks mix cost per first order with 90-day break-even without reconciling them.
to10: Fix the budget total and align the Day-30 pass/fail numbers with the 90-day contribution math so the team isn't pulled between two targets.

strength: Eight genuinely distinct concepts with customer-language hooks, a clear awareness level and single test variable each, and a first-three pick tied correctly to the data (quiet wheels, women solo, belt-skip).
mistake: The quiet-wheels Reel is buried at position three in the ranking despite being the strongest unused proof and most common review theme; also leads one concept headline with a real review line ('Fit the overhead bin...') which risks reading as a fake attributed quote.
to10: Promote the sound-led Reel to first or second, tighten primary texts to grade-7 short lines throughout, and confirm the review-quote attribution handling up front.

strength: Puts women 25 to 40 and the lift-it-alone message first, and the 5 am quiet-wheels Reel third, with a spend-per-concept testing plan (15 purchases each, ~₹63,000 total) that an owner can actually approve.
mistake: Dense table-and-rules upfront and cramped prose make primary texts harder to skim than the brief's grade-7 short-line voice wants; a few concepts (Four specs, Under ₹300) read more like product copy than customer language.
to10: Loosen the layout, rewrite primary texts as short calm lines in our voice, and add the per-concept test variable explicitly to each concept rather than only in the summary table.

strength: Every choice is tied back to the numbers: taste-test/swap openers, label after the sip, price handled on camera in scripts 1 and 2, and three genuinely different angles built from real customer lines.
mistake: Dense and slightly overloaded; the timing table plus long briefs plus a test plan pushes against the 1,300-word limit and grade-6 reading level, and a couple of spoken lines run long for their time slots.
to10: Trim to the word limit and tighten each spoken block so every line actually fits its seconds, keeping the same data-backed logic.

strength: Clean, readable, easy to shoot: clear rules, tight hook sets, and the #ad/disclosure handled cleanly; scripts read fast and match the 30-45s format.
mistake: Thinner insight and less price handling: only one script really answers the $3-a-can objection, the family script's claims moment is fumbled (it drops real fruit juice into the label read but skips the price context), and the test plan is generic with no budget or thresholds.
to10: Put price objection handling into more than one script and give the hook test real numbers, thresholds and a kill rule drawn from the 60-day data.

strength: It reads the data like an owner: it diagnoses the paused 'flip the pack' ad as fatigued rather than dead, brings it back in fresh words, and leads with it. The six angles are genuinely distinct, with counts shown and a clean 4-ad test plan.
mistake: Taste and price lines lean on review quotes, which is defensible but hedged with backup swaps — and P1's 'Every ingredient is on the front' plus P4/P5 all repeat the same 12g/no-added-sugar tag, so several texts feel closer to one another than the brief wanted.
to10: Sharper, more distinct voices for Aditya and Priya in the body copy (P5 and P6 still read like a spec list), and a bolder human taste hook that doesn't need a review quote to land.

strength: Every line is written in the buyers' own words — 'Save yourself the flip', '4 pm minus the samosa', the price said head-on — and the copy set, test cells, budget math and day-14 read are all launch-ready. It also builds a real control cell against the live ₹290 ad, which is what I'd actually do.
mistake: It launches the price-first ad as one of four while P1 and P5/P6 restate the same sugar/protein stack underneath; the 'if it wins' advice is strong but the plan slightly buries the texture angle that 14% of reviews cite.
to10: Push one more primary text on texture ('dense and chewy') into the launch four, and make each body line carry a visibly different idea rather than leaning on the same dates/protein tag.

strength: Cash figure and break-in expectation are handled honestly and consistently in bullets, specs, FAQ, the under-button line and even the measurement plan, directly targeting the top return reasons.
mistake: The under-button line omits the break-in reassurance the owner suggested ('Snug for the first week, then it settles'), so the highest-leverage return-killer is only in the body.
to10: Put the break-in line under the add-to-cart button and lead one bullet with the proof phrase 'I carry 8 cards and it still closes flat.'

strength: Highly voice-true and customer-grounded: review counts (142 'much thinner') and the 'what doesn't fit' section give it real range and credibility.
mistake: Inconsistent cash spec: the FAQ says the hidden pocket takes 'one more flat note' on top of the ~10, contradicting the bullet/spec and the owner's careful 'in total' assumption, and it changes an unverified fact rather than stating one.
to10: Lock the cash number to one consistent total, add the break-in note under the button, and confirm the SEO title length (it looks over 60 characters).

strength: Leads with the quiz-data logic and per-click revenue, then builds the whole series (default product, exit rule, sunscreen-defence email, slow-start email) around those three numbers; nails the sunscreen leak and the 61% beginner fear.
mistake: The dry/sensitive branch sends people (19%) to sunscreen as if a sunscreen were a cure for dryness, and the dryness copy is thin; also the WhatsApp only goes to non-clickers of Email 5, which slightly muddies the exit logic and assumes opt-in that may not exist.
to10: A tighter brand-voice pass on dryness/sensitivity (name a moisturiser or say plainly sunscreen is protection, not hydration), and keep the WhatsApp rule simple: opted-in, not ordered, no click needed.

strength: Warm, human, on-brand voice throughout; the three-version Email 2 and the 'no brightening serum, just Niacinamide 10%' opening are exactly the brand promise, and the start-slow rules email is clear and calm.
mistake: The 3-step routine in Email 5 stacks salicylic acid wash plus niacinamide plus sunscreen and quotes ₹1,297 — that contradicts the 'start slowly, one active' message and over-sells; also it's less explicit about per-click revenue and the exit rule is looser.
to10: Replace the 3-step upsell with the one-product-plus-sunscreen short answer, quote the right ₹698/₹998 maths, and tighten the sunscreen email to answer white cast and stickiness with the review line up front.

strength: Treats the discontinued Monsoon Dark blend and the courier-caused subscription churn as the two real causes, gives each its own track and gate, and ranks the slipping 46-90 day group first with no discount.
mistake: Pushes the cheapest and largest-lever group (46-90 days, 9,000 at risk) behind a drip of waves and buries the always-on day-28 nudge as a footnote, so the biggest repeat-rate fix reads as secondary.
to10: Lead with fixing the repeat rate at the 34-day mark as the programme's spine, then layer win-back; tighten the prose and cut the bolder pre-order section if it risks diluting focus.

strength: Reads like the brand wrote it: warm, plain, grade-7 voice, clean per-channel sequence, and it correctly puts the delivery gate and the day-28 nudge up front as the real leak.
mistake: Starts with the 91-180 day group instead of the cheaper 46-90 day at-risk group, and its lift/value table uses rounder assumptions (2 orders per buyer) that are harder to defend than per-order gross profit math.
to10: Rank the 46-90 day group first with a light no-discount reminder, and show the value math per returning order net of discount and shipping rather than stapling multi-order assumptions.

strength: Sharp diagnosis that isolates Meta and linen, and the moves are ranked, owned and sized in margin points with week-4 and week-8 checkpoints.
mistake: A few numbers are shaky: mixed margin components and a 55%-vs-59% new-customer share shift are asserted rather than reconciled.
to10: Tighten the math on the contribution baseline and reconcile the year-1 mix so every point of margin is defensible to finance.

strength: Very readable diagnostic with a payback-ladder ($71/$94) that makes the ad-spend rule intuitive and defensible.
mistake: Moves are ranked by prose, not sharp numbers; the size of each opportunity is vague and the 90-day arc is broad rather than sequenced to hit a margin target.
to10: Put a points-of-margin estimate and a first-week step against each move, and commit to a day-90 contribution-margin number.

strength: Threshold maths is sharp and honest: the ₹599 case with an explicit walk-away break-even, and it explicitly protects the serum reorder that Ishita lives on.
mistake: The serum+lip balm bundle leans on the lip balm over the actual top pair (face wash + serum), so its bundle ladder is built around a lower-value add-on rather than the proven ₹944 routine.
to10: Make face wash + serum the headline routine bundle at a modest saving with the margin shown, keep lip balm as the cart add-on, and bring COD/RTO cost into the threshold decision instead of treating every order alike.

strength: Bundles map to how customers already buy (face wash+serum, shampoo+conditioner, body lotion+body wash) with break-even maths that shows the cost of discounting existing pair buyers, plus the lip balm as threshold add-on and a COD-fee test.
mistake: Choosing to keep ₹499 as the recommendation is defensible but undersells the brief's ask to actually work the money on moving it, and the lakh-level projections carry wide ranges that read as soft.
to10: Recommend a clear threshold move (or a prepaid-only lower bar) with COD/RTO fully costed, tighten the projection ranges to one number per scenario, and say it in the owner's voice rather than in test-table shorthand.

strength: Correctly leads with the in-app checkout bug as an untested fix, sizes it in rupees, and ranks the five tests by expected impact with honest sample-size maths tied to the real traffic numbers.
mistake: The firmness test (3) is thinner than the reviews test in Output 2 and the hero/reviews test (5) mixes two changes and two metrics, muddying what a win means; nothing major otherwise.
to10: Split the combined image-plus-reviews change into one clean test, and add a short 'what we can't detect' note per test so the owner knows which small wins will read as flat.

strength: Crisp table-led plan with concrete dates, two-lane scheduling, per-test rupee projections, and a smart pointed warning that add-to-cart will fall once the delivery date shows, plus a strong bolder delivery-day move.
mistake: Metric choices are inconsistent — some tests use add-to-cart, some orders per session — and the reviews test swaps firmness (19% of chats) for reviews, slightly misfitting the firmness concern; the delivery-date test's evidence is also burdened by mixing guardrails with gross profit per order.
to10: Make the main metric consistent across page tests (or state clearly why each differs) and give each test its 'what a flat result means' sentence so the owner knows how to act.

strength: A deceptively sharp plan: it segments the flow by pincode risk with the refusal economics (₹70/₹41/₹27 loss per COD order) accounting for why each discount sits where it does, it includes holdouts so I can measure real lift, and it explicitly flags the downside of cancels and wasted discounts.
mistake: The prepaid nudge is misfiled — it puts T4 (with a ₹20/₹40 discount) and the metro nudge inside the confirmation flow but the Table says Marketing, while the metro 'normal chat' nudge has no discount — the category logic across the flow gets muddy and a reviewer might reject or recategorise. Also spends a bit of the word budget on a speculative ₹99 advance idea that could dilute priorities.
to10: Tighten the category/label discipline (Utility vs Marketing per message, discount where and why, no offer bleeding into Utility), fix the voice to feel more like ours (fewer spreadsheet-toned phrases, more Hinglish in scripts), and keep the bolder ₹99 idea as a one-line appendix rather than a full section.

strength: The most usable document: clean templates with sample values, tight flow with quiet hours, holdouts for the prepaid switch, an after-hours auto-reply plus a concrete staffing move (2 pm–midnight shift), and reply scripts that genuinely sound like Snitch with light Hinglish.
mistake: Weak on the pincode-risk economics: it lumps Tier 2 and Tier 3 together for the call/hold, and the prepaid nudge is 'ease, not a deal' so it throws away the lever that targets the highest-RTO band — it doesn't show the refusal-loss math or use a discount tiered by risk, so it underserves the core RTO problem.
to10: Segment the RTO plan explicitly (metro/Tier2/Tier3 with loss per order and a risk-tiered nudge or advance for Tier 3), show the refusal-cost math by group, and add holdouts/a cancel-cost framing so I can see what each step is worth — keeping the current clarity and voice.

strength: Calculates an ad-set-specific break-even CPA that factors in the unique AOV, COD mix, and RTO rate for every single row, then brilliantly adjusts for UTM tracking loss to give exact targets.
mistake: None significant. The assumption that prospecting captures 86% of UTMs while retargeting captures 72% is debatable, but stating the assumption up front makes it a perfectly valid approach.
to10: It is already a 10. The mathematical rigor and structural clarity are exceptional.

strength: Successfully identifies all three core signals (relaunching the paused creator ad, isolating the 25-34 women demographic, and spotting the Starter Kit as a COD trap).
mistake: The math explanation in the opening section is a bit hand-wavy, and it relies mostly on global averages rather than calculating precise bespoke margins for each ad set based on their specific metrics.
to10: Calculate exact break-even costs per ad set based on their specific average order values and RTO/COD ratios, instead of applying the global averages to most rows.

strength: Excellent grasp of unit economics, converting our AOV and margins into a clear break-even target and kill/scale rules.
mistake: Assumes setup can be completed before 'Day 1', which isn't practical if the plan starts on Monday, missing the reality of implementation timelines.
to10: More rigorous measurement methods for Day 30 like a geo-holdout, and using the exact provided customer quotes word-for-word in the creative hooks.

strength: Phenomenal translation of our data into actionable rules, such as using the organic flop watch times to create an early kill rule, and a flawless incrementality measurement plan.
mistake: None that stand out; the budget phasing, creative briefs, and measurement strategies are meticulously aligned with the brief.
to10: It is already a 10. The incorporation of a holdout test and exact customer quotes was perfect.

strength: Deep platform expertise shown through Reels text safe zones, headline character limits, and highly accurate media testing math.
mistake: None. It perfectly addressed every constraint, data signal, and requirement in the brief.
to10: It is already a 10.

strength: Strong translation of data into targeted concepts and a clear understanding of the customers' buying barriers.
mistake: Recommending only 3x CPA as the benchmark before scaling; 3x CPA without a purchase is a rule for cutting an ad, but scaling requires much more conversion volume.
to10: Include more platform-specific details like text safe zones, and refine the media buying logic for testing and scaling.

strength: Clean, easy-to-read scripts that directly address the provided data and stick perfectly to the requested timings.
mistake: Missed the opportunity to guide me on the operational side of dealing with creators.
to10: Adding standard UGC requirements like text safe zones, raw footage delivery, and usage rights.

strength: Pro-level operational instructions including text safe zones, usage rights, delivery timelines, and the brilliant '(if true)' guardrail for authentic claims.
mistake: Nothing significant; it perfectly captures the brief and anticipates my blind spots as an owner.
to10: It already hits all the marks for a 10.

strength: Very clean, modular copy that rigidly adheres to character limits, and effectively diagnoses that the top ad suffered from frequency fatigue rather than angle failure.
mistake: Missed the opportunity to use a few of the more colorful, specific persona quotes provided in the brief (like the 'samosa' line) to give the ads a punchier flavor.
to10: Integrate the target audience's colloquial quotes more deeply into the primary text, and offer a more concrete methodology for how to physically run the test in Ads Manager.

strength: Goes beyond great copywriting by providing a rigorous, professional media-buying framework, including a control cell, specific daily budget pacing, and early kill switches.
mistake: The headline 'Your 4 pm, minus the samosa' assumes slightly higher context for the image, but it's a very minor risk given the targeted audience.
to10: It's a 10. The blending of persona quotes directly into the blunt brand voice is masterful.

strength: Including a 'How to tell it worked' section showed great business acumen and an understanding of the underlying goal.
mistake: Burying the card slot break-in expectation in the description and FAQ, rather than putting it directly in the bullets or under the buy button where the early returners would definitely see it.
to10: Bringing the break-in warning above the fold and embracing the brand's calm honesty slightly more directly when discussing trade-offs.

strength: Flawlessly captured the calm, honest brand voice, especially with 'We would rather tell you now than have you send it back,' and tackled the break-in issue head-on in the bullets.
mistake: The assumption regarding the hidden pocket taking an extra note creates a slight ambiguity compared to the strict '10 notes total' limit.
to10: It is effectively a 10. Just resolving the minor cash capacity assumption with the product team would make it perfectly ready to publish.

strength: Flawless execution of dynamic content blocks to personalize the journey, and incredibly sharp data interpretation (calculating sales-per-click).
mistake: Missed the 'delight me' request to explicitly name the active and strength in the subject lines, opting for more curiosity-driven subjects instead.
to10: Injecting the product names (e.g., 'Niacinamide 10%') directly into the subject lines to fully satisfy the brand's literal, transparent approach.

strength: Clearly structures the emails and directly addresses the core objections regarding the sunscreen in a dedicated email.
mistake: Email 5 recommends a 3-step routine with Salicylic Acid and Niacinamide to the entire list, completely breaking the 'sensitive skin gets no acids' rule established in Email 2.
to10: Using dynamic blocks in Email 5 so sensitive users aren't pushed into buying acids, and incorporating the active strengths into the subject lines.

strength: The math and financial modeling are spot on, showing exact gross profit implications and incorporating a clear holdout strategy.
mistake: Missed the mark on prioritization by not treating the 46 to 90 days 'at-risk' group as the very first wave to tackle, leaving them as an afterthought beneath the main table.
to10: Making the 'slipping' 46-90 day cohort the primary focus and top priority in the campaign rollout.

strength: Nailed the exact priority order by targeting the 46-90 days drifting customers first, followed closely by the brilliant 'bolder move' idea to run a pre-order for the discontinued Monsoon Dark.
mistake: None. The execution is flawless based on the parameters.
to10: It is already a 10. The logic, math, voice, and strategic rollout sequence perfectly match the business needs.

strength: Translates complex margin and LTV math into plain English rules (like the $94 CPA cap) that a non-expert owner and the team can instantly grasp and use.
mistake: Missed adding Google's cost per first order explicitly to the weekly scorecard as requested in the brief.
to10: Adding the specific Google CPA target to the weekly scorecard to flawlessly fulfill every single detail of the prompt.

strength: Incredible analytical depth, including calculating the exact historical contribution margin and proposing a brilliant swatch kit acquisition funnel as a bolder move.
mistake: Including literal algebra (w × -11%...) in the baseline working, which violates the Grade 8 reading level and alienates a non-expert owner.
to10: Translating the complex algebraic proofs into plain English and adopting a warmer, more brand-aligned tone instead of sounding like a clinical consultant.

strength: Flawless mathematical breakdown, perfectly calculating the hidden total order volume and accurately applying RTO costs to justify a COD fee and a lip balm cart add-on.
mistake: The information density in the tables is quite high, requiring a close, careful read.
to10: It already is a 10. To make it strictly flawless, a bit more breathing room or bullet points instead of dense table text could help.

strength: Exceptionally clear formatting and brilliant logic regarding why discounting the organic 1,033 face wash + serum pairs would be a mistake.
mistake: By moving the threshold to ₹599, it only affects a very narrow slice of orders (₹499 to ₹598), missing the opportunity to fundamentally restructure the costly COD leak.
to10: Addressing the 29% COD RTO leak head-on with a specific policy change (like a COD fee) rather than relying solely on bundle step-ups.

strength: Extracting the funnel data into a table that proves in-app users have nearly the same add-to-cart intent as other users, beautifully isolating the checkout bug.
mistake: None of note; it flawlessly executed the brief's hidden traps and requirements.
to10: It is already a 10. The proposed firmness test is a perfect translation of the brand's 'plain words' requirement.

strength: Excellent statistical rigor and explicit acknowledgement of the low mobile conversion rates, plus a well-structured two-lane testing strategy.
mistake: Including specific calendar dates (e.g., 23 November) was unnecessary and assumes a timeline not provided in the brief.
to10: Showing the add-to-cart rates by browser to prove the lost checkout intent, rather than just calculating the missed revenue.

strength: Flawless translation of the data into unit economics to justify tiered prepaid discounts, along with suggesting the ₹99 advance and holdout groups.
mistake: No significant mistakes; it hit every requirement perfectly.

strength: The 'How to tell it worked' section is gold for an owner, and the conservative assumption on cash capacity protects my return rate.

strength: The 'What fits, in real life' section is excellent—it gives the customer an exact mental picture of their daily carry.

strength: Exceptional marketing logic. The use of dynamic blocks for personalization, accurate calculation of sales-per-click, and brilliant testing proposals show a true owner's mindset.
mistake: Missed the specific instruction to include the active name and strength directly in the subject lines.
to10: Include 'Niacinamide 10%' or 'SPF 50' explicitly in the subject lines as requested in the brief, rather than just in the body or preview text.

strength: Clean, easy-to-read formatting and a good initial job of separating the product recommendations based on the quiz data in Email 2.

to10: Maintain logical consistency throughout the entire flow (don't push acids to sensitive skin later on) and follow the instruction to put actives and strengths in the subject lines.

strength: Flawless handling of the data. Deduplicated the overlapping segments perfectly and identified the exact numbers for each wave.
mistake: Used a quiz for the Monsoon Dark group's first email instead of directly recommending the closest dark roast match as requested.
to10: Name the specific matched coffee right away in the G2 email draft instead of adding the friction of a survey.

strength: Excellent copywriting and voice that followed all brand rules, plus a smart callout on the cost of giving discounts to organic returners.
mistake: Completely missed sending a campaign to the 9,000 customers in the 46-90 day band. Mentioning a future Day-28 automation doesn't win back the people already drifting at day 60.
to10: Include the 46-90 day group in the actual target order as Wave 1, and ensure the segment math deduplicates ex-subscribers properly.

strength: Exceptional mathematical rigor, perfectly deducing the new vs. returning customer revenue split and exact contribution margin points.
mistake: Including an algebra equation in the middle of the text, which violates the 8th-grade reading level constraint and slows down readability.
to10: Translate the complex math into simple, plain English conclusions and soften the consulting-style tone to match the brand's warm voice.

strength: Nails the hidden 1.8% revenue impact figure perfectly, maintains the target reading level, and cleverly provides actionable page fixes for all product return reasons, not just linen.
mistake: Missed putting the explicit 'first-week step' into the ranking table itself, though it is covered adequately in the timeline section.
to10: A flawless submission as is, but adding a specific 'Week 1 Action' column to the initiatives table would make it the absolute perfect operational document.

strength: Flawless break-even math and brilliant logic on why a ₹599 threshold is smarter than ₹699 to protect the hero serum's reorder rate.
mistake: Using the lip balm as one of the three main bundles instead of a cart add-on, which missed the chance to build a body care routine.

strength: Incredible strategic alignment with the business needs: using lip balm as a cart add-on, targeting hair and body routines, and suggesting a pin-code split for shipping tests.
