to10: Double-check the arithmetic on the step-up margins and break-even targets, but otherwise, this is exactly what the business needed.

strength: The data table breakdown at the start is phenomenal, especially the brilliant deduction connecting the 4,130 in-app errors directly to the 4,800 abandoned in-app checkouts.
mistake: None. The execution is flawless, from the statistical math to the brand-specific copywriting.
to10: It is already a perfect 10.

strength: Impeccable statistical reasoning, particularly in using top-of-funnel metrics for shorter tests and providing a realistic gross profit range for the bug fix.
mistake: Splitting the reviews and hero image into two separate tests took up a slot that could have been used to address the 'firmness/foam jargon' friction point directly.
to10: Including a dedicated test for firmness that translates foam jargon into plain words, and providing a full funnel percentage breakdown to highlight the drops.

strength: Deep operational logic, such as calculating expected RTO loss by tier to set discount thresholds, using holdouts, and timing cart messages during agent working hours.
mistake: The dynamic discounts and ₹99 advance flows are brilliant but will require custom API routing rather than basic out-of-the-box WhatsApp provider tools.
to10: A brief mention of the API or tech setup required to execute the tier-specific rules and the UPI advance seamlessly.

strength: The practical suggestion to shift one agent's hours to cover the 31% evening chat wave instead of relying purely on automation.
mistake: Categorized the prepaid payment switch as a Utility template, which could trigger Meta rejection, and missed the opportunity to offer a targeted incentive for Tier 3.
to10: Differentiating the COD confirmation flows more aggressively for Tier 3 right from the start, and placing the prepaid nudge in the Marketing category.

strength: Keeps the second-biggest buyer doubt (firmness, 19% of chats) as its own test, and every test is tied to a line of evidence plus an honest MDE.
mistake: Test 5 bundles two separate changes (hero image and reviews placement), so even if it wins I cannot tell which change earned it.
to10: Split Test 5 into two changes, and use add-to-cart as the main metric on the size and EMI tests (with orders as guardrail) so the answer does not need four weeks and a 10-12% lift to show up.

strength: Operator-ready: the broken in-app checkout is fixed first with the money on it (about 560 orders, roughly 34 lakh gross margin), and every test carries run dates, a detectable effect and a rupee projection.
mistake: Drops firmness as its own test even though it is 19% of chats and the named objection ('What if it's too soft for us?'), and runs the hero-image test over 21 Dec-3 Jan when traffic is unrepresentative.
to10: Give firmness its own ranked test, keep the hero image test inside a normal trading window, and put the trial and delivery microcopy in brand words so it ships as written.

strength: Strong operational detail: clean templates, quiet hours, after-hours bot, and most RTO/chat numbers are right.
mistake: The prepaid nudge has no incentive and is filed as Utility, so it misses the tier-3 switch lever and risks Meta reclassification.
to10: Add a tier-specific prepaid incentive or advance, correct it to Marketing, resolve the tier-2/3 hold contradiction, and add a final auto-cancel rule.

strength: Tiered RTO plan with prepaid incentives and calls where refusal cost is highest, plus net-savings holdout discipline and a bold ₹99 advance test.
mistake: T5 assumes COD is available on every abandoned cart; it needs a non-COD pincode variant, and the weekly scorecard omits after-hours response time.
to10: Add the cart template fallback for non-COD pincodes, add after-hours response time to the scorecard, and tighten the weekly baseline rounding.

strength: Very production-ready: exact scenes, headlines, safe zones, approved-claim guardrails, and test budgets the team could execute tomorrow.
mistake: It never uses the 41+ audience, which is the most expensive segment at ₹2,188 per purchase, and its women-first prioritisation is arguable rather than decisive.
to10: Add a 41+ proof concept or retargeting use, sharpen the purchase-share insight for women, and trim the spec recitation in primary text for a calmer voice.

strength: Sharpest strategic read: it spots the women 25-40 purchase-share gap, uses the 41+ proof opportunity, and keeps all eight concepts distinct and easy to approve.
mistake: Less production-ready than it could be: no explicit headlines or safe-zone specs, and Concept 1 says 'Cabin size' / 'Zero belt time' where the approved cabin-limit line would be safer.
to10: Add exact headlines, aspect-ratio/safe-zone notes, and tighten claims so every concept uses 'fits most Indian domestic airline cabin limits' where size is implied.

strength: Reads the past 90 days correctly: the front-of-pack ad was tired, not dead, and taste is the never-run proof. The layout is the easiest of the two to review, and the judgement rules (cost per purchase, swap before frequency 3.5) are right.
mistake: Only five real angles, not six: P1 and P5 are the same transparency idea, P6 fuses price with the 4 pm scene, and there is no straight protein or office-snack text. So launch ad D tests price and the 4 pm segment at once and proves neither, and the set has a duplicate.
to10: Make P5 a clean 4 pm/Priya text, make P6 price-only, add a straight protein angle, and give the first four a runnable test: a control cell, a daily budget, and a purchase count needed to call a winner.

strength: Six genuinely different angles in customers' own words, plus a test you can hand to a media buyer today: control cell copying the live ₹290 ad, ₹1,200 a day per cell, 58 vs 44 purchases at your known costs, an early-cut rule, a 20% decision rule, fatigue at 3.5 and UTMs. The ₹6,333 a day figure is derived correctly from the spend table, and ₹90 a bar is right.
mistake: Headlines drift off the angle being tested: ad D pairs a no-added-sugar primary with 'Ingredients on the front', and ad B pairs taste with '12 g protein per bar'. That blurs what each cell proves, and the price ad asserts ₹90 without a value comparison.
to10: Match each headline to the angle its primary text is testing so each cell answers one question, tighten the copy to stay comfortably under the word cap, and give the ₹90 line one honest everyday comparison.

strength: Sharp, concise copy set with a strong diagnosis of the paused winner and the untapped taste gap, plus a legal fallback if review quotes are not allowed.
mistake: Misses a dedicated protein-number angle and a standalone 4 pm office angle, and misstates Meta's headline/description limits as 27 characters.
to10: Cover all six requested angles distinctly, correct the Meta display limits, and add a control or benchmark to the launch test plan.

strength: Covers all six angles in buyer language and gives a genuinely actionable test design with a control, budget, cut rules, and tracking.
mistake: Runs long against the 1,000-word cap, overstates Meta's headline/description limits, and relies on review quotes without a fallback if legal blocks them.
to10: Trim it under 1,000 words, fix the Meta display limits, and add a no-review-quote backup while keeping the test rigor.

strength: Clean, brand-voiced page that puts cash and break-in upfront and names trade-offs honestly.
mistake: Risks overstating capacity: adding a hidden-pocket note and implying 12 cards plus 10 notes at 14 mm; SEO title is also over 60 characters.
to10: Use only sourced capacity/thickness combinations, make the cash total conservative, and add a simple return-rate measurement plan.

strength: Conservative cash-capacity handling plus a concrete return-rate measurement plan and fallback make it directly usable for the owner’s goal.
mistake: Invents an approximate 10 to 11 mm thickness for 6 or 7 cards with cash, and the measurement section is internal, not publish-ready page copy.
to10: Stick strictly to sourced numbers and clearly separate internal measurement notes from the final customer-facing page.

strength: Turns the quiz and product data into a branched, practical flow: one matched product first, a real answer to the sunscreen objections, and a clear slow-start plan.
mistake: The generic 'use it every other night' line in Email 5 and the WhatsApp contradicts the sunscreen-only path for dry or sensitive subscribers; sunscreen is a morning step, not an every-other-night active.
to10: Fix the product-specific usage lines so sunscreen is always every morning, trim it to the 1,800-word limit, and swap in the real Klaviyo variables and links.

strength: Good instinct to structure the flow around the data: sunscreen leak, quiz-based product match, and a dedicated beginner-safety email.
mistake: Email 5 pushes all three products as a universal 3-step routine, including salicylic acid face wash twice daily, which contradicts the start-slow, one-active-at-a-time advice and the sensitive-skin path.
to10: Rewrite Email 5 to branch by quiz answer and keep the routine to one active plus sunscreen where appropriate; remove even negative mentions of 'brightening' and 'clear skin'; make the WhatsApp usage product-specific; and trim to the brief.

strength: It works the groups in the order my data argues for — slipping 46-90 day buyers first with no discount, then a named Monsoon Dark track, then ex-subscribers behind a hard delivery gate — and every row of the money table reconciles back to ₹557/₹442/₹385 per order.
mistake: It never states the minimum lift each group needs to break even, which is the one measuring item I asked for; the ₹535 profit it uses for ex-subscribers is unexplained, and the ₹14,000 WhatsApp figure is a round guess.
to10: Add the break-even lift per group next to the assumed lift, explain the ₹535 ex-subscriber number (or use ₹385/₹557 as elsewhere), and show reach including WhatsApp opt-ins rather than email alone.

strength: The diagnosis that most lapsed buyers did not leave over price — something broke — plus the day-28 'running low' nudge as the cheapest fix for a repeat rate falling from 34% to 28%; the cancel-reason split (late, too much, price, moving) is genuinely useful.
mistake: It ranks 91-180 day buyers first and demotes the 46-90 day 'at risk' group to a side note, against the brief; and group A's 13,100 still contains the 900 Monsoon Dark buyers it mails separately and the subscribers it says it pulled out, so people get two sequences.
to10: Put the 46-90 day group first as its own wave with dates, de-duplicate group A against the Monsoon Dark and subscriber lists, and build the value case on ₹557/₹442/₹385 per order instead of assuming two to four orders per win-back.

strength: The copy. Hooks are lifted from real review and survey lines and the primary text is written in our short-line, grade-7 voice ('Two flights a month. Zero belt time. Land. Roll. Leave.'). The data read up top is clean: 70% of spend, 18% of spend for women at 26% of purchases (104 of 396), and the ₹292-a-trip maths all check out.
mistake: The measurement advice is too thin to act on: telling me to judge each concept after three times blended cost per purchase, about ₹4,500, is roughly three purchases. That is noise, and I would cut good creative or scale bad creative on it. It also says nothing about the 60 front-pocket reviews, so a big known objection goes unanswered.
to10: Replace the ₹4,500 threshold with a purchase-count rule (about 15 purchases or ~₹20,000+ per concept, sized to each audience's current cost per purchase) and a stop rule. Add the front-pocket objection to the assumptions, or a scene showing what the bag does have. Tighten concepts 6 and 7 so they are not the weakest of the eight.

strength: It reads like a working creative brief: pixel sizes, safe zones, headline character counts (all counted correctly), scene beats to the second, and a test plan with real budgets — 15 purchases per concept, ₹63,000 total, about a tenth of last month's spend — plus a stop rule. And it is the only one that catches both bits of bad news, scuffs on dark shells and the missing front pocket, and turns them into rules for the shoot.
mistake: It mangles our line: 'Built for the way you travel now' instead of 'Built for the way you travel now.' Small, but it is our line. The primary texts also run long and dense for a brand that says short lines, and it puts the line taking 70% of spend second rather than first.
to10: Restore the brand line exactly, break the primary text into short lines, and lead with the belt-skip concept while keeping the women-first argument as the budget-scale case. Add one concept for the 41-plus group (₹2,188 per purchase) so all three audience rows are addressed.

strength: Calls the in-app checkout bug first, sizes the money, and gives five ranked tests with honest MDEs and sensible metric choices.
mistake: Tests 1 and 2 overlap and the interaction handling is loose; firmness is left as a review-move test rather than a direct firmness answer.
to10: Add an explicit assumptions and A/A split-hygiene block, tighten the overlapping-test read or sequence them, and test a plain firmness explainer directly.

strength: Excellent diagnostic table; ties the pop-up errors to the exact in-app checkout gap and gives a clear schedule, A/A check and tracking plan.
mistake: Bundles hero image and review reordering into one test, so a win cannot be attributed; and uses orders rather than add-to-cart for the size test, making it slower and less sensitive.
to10: Split the hero and review changes into separate tests, switch the size test to add-to-cart with orders as guardrail, and keep the clean schedule and A/A check.

strength: It makes a clear, rupee-backed decision for every ad set and a precise budget that adds up, with the relaunch of the paused creator video as the first move.
mistake: The break-even calculation for ASC uses a blended profit per order (₹339) that does not reflect its actual COD and RTO mix, potentially misjudging its profitability.
to10: A clear, step-by-step implementation timeline for Monday's actions and a simple table of projected weekly profit impact from each decision.

strength: The dual break-even lines (safe and break-even) make the attribution haircut practical and easy to apply.
mistake: Its budget allocation for ASC is more aggressive and lacks a clear daily ramp schedule, risking overspend if performance does not improve immediately.
to10: A more detailed daily budget plan for ASC with clear gates and a contingency if it fails to hit targets, plus a clearer projection of profit impact.

strength: Every rule traces back to my own numbers: target $38 from the 90-day break-even, $29 problem-first vs $51 mission-first, 11.4s vs 2.8s watch times, and a phased budget plus kill/scale rules in real dollars that add to $30,000.
mistake: The setup week has no spend buffer or explicit fallback if the pixel or Events API test fails, so a day-1 slip could quietly eat the test window; also '21+' targeting is looser than the 30-something buyer profile.
to10: A named owner and date for each setup step with a hard go/no-go on the test order, plus the day-30 holdout or baseline comparison spelled out so I can trust the pass/fail rather than a single survey.

strength: Puts the money math on one screen, translates it into concrete thresholds (learning bar $136/day, $114 kill spend), and adds a bolder geo-holdout test plus a clean rule for what happens when TikTok's numbers and Shopify disagree.
mistake: The bold holdout is introduced as a real recommendation without resolving the conflict between 'hold $1,000 a day' and 'return $4,750 to Meta,' and giving three reads equal weight risks analysis paralysis; the unallocated risk if the test order fails is also thin.
to10: Lock the holdout decision into the Monday plan with one clear fallback budget, and tighten the day-30 rules to a single primary measure (store-tagged new customers) so the team can't cherry-pick the read that looks best.

strength: Ties every concept to a data signal (quiet wheels, women solo, belt-skip), keeps claims inside the approved specs, and writes primary text in the brand voice with review-language hooks.
mistake: A few execution lines drift from the approved claims - 'Soft morning light' scenes fine, but 'Warranty and returns are on our site' is borderline and the ₹292-per-trip static is a weaker bet than the proof carousel; also the 5 am Reel needs a stronger sound-off fallback.
to10: Explicit per-concept test metric and budget already present; add one or two bolder format risks (UGC creator testimonial, comparison of colours) and a tighter scratch-objection concept that leads lighter colours by default across all eight.

strength: Sharp, disciplined structure with spec grid, exact spend maths for the test budget, and honest handling of scuffs and front-pocket gaps up front.
mistake: Format risks are modest - several concepts (spec demo, price static, gift static) are still close to the flat product-on-colour family, and the 'four specs' reel is more comparison-proof than a distinct angle, so range feels narrower than promised.
to10: More genuinely different formats (sound-led Reel given its full due, a creator selfie video, a real customer testimonial) and primary text that sounds less like a spec sheet and more like the brand's calm voice.

strength: Clean, shootable scripts built on the real data: taste-first openers, the 3 pm hook, price handled head-on, disclosure written into every brief.
mistake: Script 3's hook leads on the kids line while the label moment sits mid-script; also the disclosure instruction ('start the caption with #ad') is thinner than platform toggles need, and the briefs are good but a shade wordier than they need to be.
to10: Tighten script 3 so the label is not the spine of a family ad, add the on-screen 'Ad' frame rule and delivered-asset specs (captions, safe zones, raw clips) from the other version, and give each hook a one-word note on what single thing it changes.

strength: Reads like a producer's plan: opening-style table with cost per purchase, price math on screen, a real test budget with cut rules, and the strongest creator briefs and delivery specs of the two.
mistake: The spoken disclosure lines ('Olipop paid me for this one', 'Olipop paid me to make this') are clunky and repeated mid-ad; the on-screen 'Ad' from frame one plus the toggle is the compliant part, and the extra spoken plugs hurt the voice. Script 1 also puts a claim before the full reveal rhythm settles.
to10: Drop the awkward spoken payment lines to a single natural mention early, keep the on-screen Ad and toggles, and rewrite script 3 so the dad's line is an observation after the kids' reaction rather than a claim lead-in.

strength: Nails the strategy: revives the fatigued ₹210 winner with fresh words, leads with the never-run taste review, and takes on the ₹90 price objection directly, all in your blunt voice with char counts.
mistake: Some taste/texture primary texts lean on review quotes as if they were proof rather than flagging the legal risk up front (it does offer backups, but P2/P3 could read as implied claims), and the launch plan under-specifies budget/read rules compared with what a real test needs.
to10: Add a clean, testable budget and stopping rule like Output 2, and tighten the review-quote handling so no ad could be mistaken for a brand claim.

strength: Equally sharp strategy but more launch-ready: a real 5-cell test with a live-ad control, budget per cell, early-cut and 20%-win rules, fatigue trigger, and UTM tracking, plus a samosa line straight from Priya's mouth.
mistake: The invented ₹6,000/day budget and ₹84,000 test spend are assumptions dressed as near-facts; if wrong they could mislead, though clearly labeled assumptions.
to10: Trim the assumed budget into an explicit 'scale to your spend' note and make the control-cell logic impossible to misread.

strength: Puts the real numbers (10 notes, 5-12 cards, 10/14 mm) and honest trade-offs in calm brand voice right above the fold, and handles the break-in and cash returns head-on.
mistake: Buries the return-cutting line under the button and gives the buyer no obvious next step for the 'too much cash' case, and the assumptions section loads the owner with follow-up questions rather than confidence.
to10: Move the break-in and cash-capacity reassurance into the line under the add-to-cart button, add a single graceful 'pick a bigger wallet if you carry a lot of cash' link beside the bullets, and trim the assumptions to one line.

strength: Same honest numbers and brand voice, but adds a 'browse our other wallets' escape hatch for the cash-heavy buyer, puts the return-cutting line right under the button, and gives the owner a simple way to check it worked with today's figures.
mistake: The 'how to tell it worked' section and link block edge toward strategy notes rather than page copy, and the subtitle repeats the opening line almost exactly as Output 1, so less differentiation on the very top line.
to10: Keep the measurement plan as a separate short note rather than inside the deliverable, and sharpen the subtitle so it leads with the slim number or the proof line instead of a straight spec list.

strength: Uses the real numbers to drive decisions (niacinamide's 8% vs sunscreen's 2.2%, 44% dark spots, 61% new to actives) and the conditional product matching plus sunscreen-doubt email directly answers Sneha's and Arjun's fears.
mistake: Runs slightly long (the tests/projection section and per-click revenue math push past the 1,800-word brief) and the product-match logic lumps in 'no answer' with dark spots, which could mis-aim some subscribers.
to10: Trim the projected-revenue and A/B math to fit the word limit, and make the 'no answer' path a gentle 'tell us your concern' nudge rather than defaulting to niacinamide.

strength: Clean, calm, on-brand copy with clear three-version personalisation and a well-placed sunscreen-questions email; easy to read and close to sendable.
mistake: Email 5 pushes a fixed 3-step routine (wash + niacinamide + sunscreen together) that contradicts the brand's own 'one active at a time, start slowly' rule and ignores each person's quiz answer; the WhatsApp also lacks a concrete product pick.
to10: Make the closing email follow the quiz answer with a two-step routine and a starter pick, and keep the 'add one at a time' teaching consistent with it.

strength: It finds the real stories in the data (the retired Monsoon Dark blend, the courier-caused subscription leak) and builds a ranked, costed, holdout-measured programme around them, with drafts that sound like us and never guilt-trip.
mistake: The projected gross-profit range is built on assumed extra-return rates with thin justification, and the G6 profit-each figure (₹535) is not explained against the offer logic, so a careful reader has to trust rather than verify.
to10: Show the arithmetic behind every assumed lift and profit-per-order figure (including G6) and give one or two sentences on how the ranges were sized, so I can defend the number to my founder without reworking it.

strength: Strong narrative on fixing the reason before discounting, a clear delivery gate for ex-subscribers, and a sensible day-28 'running low' nudge to stop the repeat-rate slide.
mistake: Priorities and numbers are shaky: it puts the 91-180 day group first instead of the cheaper 46-90 day at-risk group, and its valuation stacks an unexplained ₹999/₹2,113 per-customer assumption on top of assumed lifts, giving an optimistic ₹8.5 lakh I cannot verify.
to10: Reorder to start with the 46-90 day at-risk group, show lift assumptions against a break-even table, and break the 12-month value into first-order gross profit net of discount and messaging cost so the headline number is auditable.

strength: Crystal-clear diagnosis that isolates Meta as the cost problem and linen as the product leak, with a simple $94 payback rule and a tight ranked move list an owner can act on Monday.
mistake: No overall contribution-margin figure or baseline, so the board's actual ask (contribution margin up this year) is tracked only as a vague 'up every month' rather than a real number and target.
to10: Add the baseline and day-90 target for contribution margin as a percent of revenue, and size each move in dollars or points of margin so the ranking can be checked.

strength: Translates everything into points of contribution margin with explicit low/likely/high ranges, and gives the owner a real baseline (7.8% to 13.6%) plus a day-90 target and per-move sizing, including a bold swatch-kit test.
mistake: Buries and over-models the numbers: the contribution derivation rests on unstated-but-load-bearing assumptions (order values flat, email mix), the 'at least $94' repeat value is undercounted, and the density of points-of-margin math makes it harder to skim than the plan it is replacing.
to10: Lead with one plain contribution-margin line and slide the point-level math to an appendix, fix the repeat-value phrasing, and simplify the presentation so a non-expert can read it in five minutes.

strength: A complete, actionable plan: bundles, a threshold move with the money worked out, and a sequenced test — all written in plain language I could hand to my team.
mistake: Its bundle ladder pushes the shampoo duo and a serum-plus-lip-balm step-up over the routine bundle customers already buy; treating the ₹499–598 slice as 'about 6%' is a guess dressed as a number, and the threshold math (₹109 profit per add-on) looks optimistic.
to10: Build bundle one on the face wash + serum pair customers already buy (₹944 at list, priced near ₹849), show the margin and the money, and use COD/RTO to justify a COD-specific fee rather than only the threshold move.

strength: It reasons from my own purchase data — builds the lead bundle on the top pair, keeps ₹499 because it sits exactly where COD refusals fall, and finds the real leak in under-₹499 COD orders, with a lip balm cart fix and a COD fee idea.
mistake: The 'bolder move' COD fee is a separate big decision that gets only a short section and could complicate the test plan; the body duo is weaker than the face wash + serum routine the brief points to, and some projections are wide ranges rather than firm numbers.
to10: Put the face wash + serum routine (around ₹849) as bundle one with full margin maths, and fully spec the COD fee as its own step with expected RTO savings and a guardrail on new customers.

strength: Puts the in-app checkout bug first with the money attached, then ranks five tests that each trace to a line of evidence, with honest small-effect maths and a firm ship-without-testing list.
mistake: The two-lane schedule and 75%-ish traffic days are busy, and the 'smallest effect' figures are stated confidently without showing the calculation; also the hero image test is low-evidence filler.
to10: Show the sample-size arithmetic, trim to four tests plus the bug, and add exact in-voice copy strings for the delivery and trial lines.

strength: Opens with a clean segmented funnel table that proves the bug in one glance, quantifies it to ₹34 lakh margin, and offers five distinct ideas including a firmness bar the other answer missed.
mistake: Test 5 bundles two separate changes (hero image and reviews) into one test, so the winner is unreadable, and the schedule stretches to 11 weeks which is slower than needed.
to10: Split the bundled test, tighten the calendar, and put more of the brand's friendly voice into the change and hypothesis lines.

strength: Tier-specific treatment of COD confirmation with the expected-loss math per pincode band, plus explicit holdouts so the owner can measure real savings.
mistake: Some template copy is a bit mechanical and a couple of bodies carry more than one action (e.g. T8), and the ₹99 advance section, while flagged as risky, sits close to the plan without an explicit 'do not run yet' label.
to10: Tighten template copy to Snitch's bold, short voice with one action per message, and pull the bolder ₹99 move into a clearly marked 'test later' box with a stop rule spelled out up front.

strength: Cleanest, most ready-to-submit templates and scripts in a genuinely Snitch voice, with crisp timing and quiet hours; also strong on after-hours staffing fix.
mistake: Treats COD confirmation more uniformly and only applies the 48-hour hold to Tier 3 late in the flow; the RTO-by-tier money is stated but not used to shape discounts or nudges per band, and the pay_online template is filed as Utility despite containing an incentive-ish framing.
to10: Make the pincode-tier risk the backbone of the confirmation and prepaid flows (different nudges, call rules, hold timing per band), and re-check template categories so nothing marketing-like sits in Utility.

strength: Ties every recommendation to the owner's numbers, separates what is proved from what needs checking, and gives ranked moves with owners, gain/effort, stop items and a runnable scorecard.
mistake: The contribution and move-lift forecasts rest on several assumptions and look more certain than the data supports; the team should label and validate them before treating them as targets.
to10: Add a one-page owner summary and first-week checklist, simplify the baseline math for the team, and flag every projection as an assumption to validate.

strength: Very readable and brand-aware: it nails the core diagnosis, keeps the customer language, and gives a practical 90-day sequence with sensible stops.
mistake: The scorecard and move ranking are not operational enough: there is no numeric contribution baseline or day-90 target, no gain/effort scoring, and vague targets like 'up every month' or 'pre-January level' instead of action thresholds.
to10: Quantify the contribution baseline and each move's gross-profit impact and effort, add weekly action thresholds and exact day-90 targets, and keep the plain-language voice.

strength: It uses the ad data to force taste-first openings, answers the $3-a-can objection directly, and gives the team production, disclosure and test rules they can act on tomorrow.
mistake: The plan says every script answers '$3 a can' on camera, but only Script 2 does; Scripts 1 and 3 show $35.99 but not the per-can price or a spoken price answer.
to10: Make the $3/can price answer explicit in every script, or stop claiming it is, and trim the extra rules so the team gets one tight page plus the three scripts.

strength: The scripts are clean, natural and easy to shoot, with hooks taken from customer language and creator briefs that give the right amount of freedom.
mistake: Script 3's alternate hook changes the whole scene, so it cannot be tested as a first-3-seconds-only hook; the test plan also has no clear budget or decision thresholds.
to10: Add specific test budgets and cut/scale thresholds, keep every alternate hook to a true first-3-second change, and include spoken disclosure plus delivery and rights details.

strength: It builds bundles from the pairs customers already buy, then ties the shipping decision to COD/RTO economics with break-evens and a practical test plan.
mistake: Some projection maths is compressed and slightly opaque, especially the Glow Routine break-even increment and the lip-balm cart lift, so the team would need to re-check those assumptions before quoting them.
to10: A one-page reconciliation table showing each bundle’s margin, break-even, threshold effect and COD impact, with cleaner assumptions and no ambiguous incremental-profit figures.

strength: The serum-to-serum-plus-lip-to-routine ladder is a strong merchandising idea and the assumptions are stated clearly.
mistake: The ₹599 threshold maths is materially off: it assumes only about 1,000 affected orders versus a likely much larger slice, and it counts lip-balm margin as gain while ignoring the lost ₹49 shipping fee, so the +₹28,000/month projection is not reliable.
to10: Rebuild the threshold P&L from the order export, net off lost shipping fees and COD RTO, and add explicit COD handling plus a clearer body/second-category bundle.
